docs.title: Pacific Northwest Field Manual
docs.text: A master database for backcountry fishing, upland bird hunting, hiking, dispersed camping, and astronomy. Organized by geographic corridor so a single region page surfaces every nearby spot regardless of activity.

docs.title: Highway 2 Corridor Overview
docs.text:
• Primary Passes: Northwest Forest Pass, Discover Pass (State Parks/WDFW lands near Gold Bar/Index).
  • Key Targets: Native Coastal Cutthroat, stocked Rainbows, and Brook Trout in high-alpine cirques.
  • Seasonality: Most alpine lakes ice out late May / early June. Lower-elevation lakes fishable earlier.

docs.title: Barclay Lake
docs.text: Barclay sits in a heavily timbered pocket at the base of Baring Mountain, whose north face climbs nearly 3,000 ft straight up out of the water in a wall of dark rock. The approach is a flat, well-graded forest walk — one of the easiest "real" hikes in the Hwy 2 corridor — winding through mossy second-growth hemlock and Western redcedar. The lake itself is long and shallow on the entry end, deepening as the trail follows the north shore. Old log jams near the outlet and along the timbered bank give you stable platforms to cast from without bushwhacking. Because the trailhead is so accessible, it's popular as a family backpack and gets steady weekend pressure — go midweek or early. Rainbows and brookies share the water; pan-fryers are the rule, not lunkers.

docs.title: Lake Serene
docs.text: Serene is locked into a granite cirque directly beneath the sheer 3,000-ft north face of Mt. Index — possibly the most dramatic alpine setting on Hwy 2. The trail is a workout: 3.6 miles and 2,000 ft of gain, much of it on engineered stairs and switchbacks chiseled out of the cliff bands. The lake stays cold all summer because the wall above shadows it for half the day. Shore access is largely limited to "Lunch Rock," a flat outcrop on the south shore that juts out over the drop-off and serves as the de facto fishing pier. Camping isn't allowed, so this is a day trip — start early. Fishing-wise this is a "scenic with bonus fishing" outing more than a destination angling lake; the rainbows are there but the place is really about the setting and the effort.

docs.title: Lake Valhalla
docs.text: Valhalla sits just below the crest of the Cascades near Stevens Pass, a true subalpine lake tucked under the granite shoulder of Lichtenberg Mountain. The Pacific Crest Trail traces its eastern edge, so you'll share the basin with thru-hikers in late summer. Unlike most cirque lakes, Valhalla has a long sandy beach on its northeast shore — a rarity in the Cascades and the main reason it's so shore-fishable. The water deepens fast off the beach, putting cruising trout within easy casting range without a boat. Westslope cutthroat and rainbow are both present and willing on small spinners or a bubble-and-fly rig. The Smith Brook approach is moderate; the gain is real but spread over 3.5 miles, and the basin's openness makes the final descent feel like a reward.

docs.title: SF Skykomish Tributaries — Beckler, Foss, Rapid, Miller Rivers
docs.text: WDFW manages four small-to-medium freestone tributaries of the South Fork Skykomish as a single regulatory group: Beckler, Foss, Rapid, and Miller rivers. All four sit just east of the town of Skykomish off Hwy 2, all four flow cold and clear off the high country between Stevens Pass and the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and all four share the same rules. They're not destination water in the way the mainstem Skykomish is — these are small, walkable, brushy mountain streams that reward an angler willing to bushwhack a bit. The fishery is resident rainbow and coastal cutthroat with the occasional mountain whitefish; bull trout are also present and must be released, system-wide and ESA-listed. The short open season (just over six weeks) and selective gear rules narrow the audience considerably — but if you're in the corridor for a Barclay/Wallace/Serene trip, an evening or morning on one of these is an easy add-on.

docs.title: What "Selective Gear Rules" actually means
docs.text:
• Single-point barbless hooks only (pinch flat or replace trebles)
  • No bait of any kind — including scented baits (PowerBait, Mice Tails, Trout Worms, Power Eggs), salmon eggs, sand shrimp, worms
  • Artificial flies and lures only

docs.title: Bull Trout
docs.text:
• Present in the Skykomish system; catch-and-release statewide, ESA-listed
  • ID: white-edged dorsal/anal/pelvic fins, no black spots on the dorsal fin (vs brook trout which have black markings on dorsal)
  • When in doubt → release

docs.title: Tackle (the constraint-shaped kit)
docs.text:
✅ Will work: * Inline spinners (Rooster Tails, Mepps Aglia #0–#1, Panther Martin) — with trebles crushed barbless OR replaced with single siwash hooks (~$0.50 each at any tackle shop) * Small spoons (Kastmaster 1/12–1/8 oz, Little Cleo) — same hook conversion * Bubble + fly rig — fits selective gear cleanly. Small dries (Parachute Adams, Elk Hair Caddis) or wets (soft hackles, small streamers) * Existing Fenwick 6.5' Light + Okuma 2500 + 4 lb fluoro leader = right setup, no change needed

❌ Leave in the car: * PowerBait dough / Power Eggs / Mice Tails / Trout Worms — all scented, all illegal here * Gulp! / Berkley scented soft plastics — same * Sand shrimp, worms, salmon eggs * Anything with treble hooks unless converted

docs.title: Scouting Report
docs.text:
• Reading the water: Cast upstream and slightly across; retrieve back with the current. Trout hold at heads/tails of pools, behind boulders, and in seams where fast water meets slow.
  • 14" minimum is real: Most resident cutthroat in these streams run 8–12". You'll catch fish, but keepers (cutthroat and wild rainbow ≥14") are uncommon. Hatchery rainbows (fin-clipped) follow the lower statewide minimum, but stocking density on these tribs is modest.
  • Best windows: First two weeks of season after the runoff drops and clears; then mornings/evenings in late June.
  • Bushwhack factor: Plenty of brush. Wear pants, bring polarized glasses, and a long-billed hat for casting under cover.

docs.title: Wallace Lake
docs.text: Wallace sits well above the popular Wallace Falls day-hike traffic, deep enough into the timber that the basin feels genuinely backcountry despite being inside a state park. The approach uses the Greg Ball Trail — an old logging rail grade that's smooth and steady, making the 4.5 miles feel shorter than the distance suggests. The lake is unusual for the Cascades in that it holds lake trout (mackinaw) alongside rainbow and brook trout; the mackinaw run deep, so shore anglers mostly tag the rainbows and brookies. Stream inlets and outlets are the productive zones, with gravel bars and downed logs giving you stable platforms to cast from. Backcountry sites at Wallace and nearby Jay Lake mean you can stretch this into an overnight, but the permit goes through the state-park call-in number at (360) 793-0420. Open year-round and two-pole legal — a rare combination in WA.

docs.title: Ashland Lakes
docs.text: The Ashland Lakes are a pair of small, dark waters in the Morningstar Natural Resources Conservation Area — DNR land, not USFS, which is why the pass is Discover and not Northwest Forest. The basin sits in the Puget Sound Convergence Zone and catches an unusual amount of rain and snow, leaving the lakes stained tannic from decaying old-growth duff. The trail is heavily boardwalked to protect the surrounding wetlands; the result is mud-free, structured access over otherwise impossible-to-walk boggy shoreline. Brook trout dominate, with occasional cutthroat stockings, and the fish tend to hold near the bottom in the dark water — weight your bait or run small streamers slow. Upper Ashland is 2.2 miles in with a mild 400 ft of climb; Lower is a few hundred yards earlier. Wooden tent platforms scattered near the lakes make this a quiet overnight option that almost nobody pressures.

docs.title: Boardman Lake
docs.text: Boardman sits in a cirque on the north slope of Bald Mountain, ringed by old-growth cedars and Pacific silver fir thick enough to swallow the basin whole. The approach is just one mile, but the density of the timber and the way the trail drops into the cirque make it feel like a real backcountry outing. The trail passes small, marshy Lake Evan a few minutes in — a decent warm-up cast if Boardman is busy. A large log jam at the outlet creek serves as the main casting platform: stable, brush-free, and right above the drop-off. Faint social paths trace the east and north shores out to a few additional spots, but bushwhacking off them gets gnarly quickly. Rainbow and brook trout are the residents and aren't picky; this is a good "low investment, real return" lake for an afternoon.

docs.title: Umtanum Creek / Yakima River Canyon
docs.text:
The Yakima River Canyon along Hwy 821 between Ellensburg and Yakima is a scenic eastside trip destination — Yakima River blue-ribbon trout fishing, bighorn sheep on the canyon walls, the Umtanum Creek Trail, and Big Pines BLM camping all in one corridor. The canyon is part of the Wenas Wildlife Area managed by WDFW.

⚠ Quail-hunting reality check (current, 2025–26): This page was originally framed as a "classic fall quail hunt." Subsequent verification against WDFW District 8 prospects (Aug 2025) shows that framing is wrong for current conditions — see Current Population Status below. As of 2026, treat the canyon as a fishing/scenery destination with bonus bird opportunity, not a quail-focused trip. For an actual quail-focused trip, see Better Alternatives section.

docs.title: Current Population Status
docs.text:
The reality, per WDFW District 8 Hunting Prospects (Aug 2025), verbatim:

"Most of the quail habitat in the Wenas Wildlife Area has burned in recent years."

"Quail in riparian draws surrounded by sagebrush are getting hard to find."

"The best chance of finding good coveys will be near rivers and irrigated land."

2024 Black Canyon Fire — GMU 340 & 342 (Manastash and Umtanum): burned over 10,000 acres of the Wenas Wildlife Area. Recovery on shrub-steppe / riparian habitat is multi-year; the burned portions will not be productive quail habitat in 2026.

Harvest trend: District 8 quail harvest crashed in 2021 (lowest harvest ever recorded) and has stayed flat at that low level. Combined causes: deep snow 2016–17, drought 2020–22, annual fires.

Season dates (verify current pamphlet): * California (Valley) Quail: typically mid-Oct – mid-Jan (2025–26 was Oct 18 – Jan 19), daily limit 3, possession 15. * Yakama Nation extended season Jan 1–15 in the lower Yakima Corridor: 10 daily / 30 possession — see Yakama Nation note below.

docs.title: Better Alternatives
docs.text:
For a 2026 quail-focused trip with a real density of birds, the WDFW biologist explicitly recommends away from Wenas/Umtanum:

  1. Yakama Nation lower Yakima River corridor — the District 8 quail recommendation. Tribal permit required; call 509-865-5121 ext. 6307 for current rules. The extended Jan 1–15 season with 10-bird limit is the real prize.
  2. Columbia Basin — Quincy + Desert Wildlife Areas (Grant County) — WDFW's #2 quail county statewide, ~3–4 hrs from Shoreline. Agricultural / CRP / irrigation-ditch habitat unaffected by the Wenas fires. The lower-risk pivot if Yakama Nation permits are too much hassle.
  3. Sunnyside-Snake River Wildlife Area — public, but WDFW data: 87% hunters unsuccessful, 0.16 birds/day. A real option, but a poor one.

If you're already committed to the canyon for other reasons (fishing, scenery, bighorn viewing, Big Pines camping), the bird opportunity here is now bonus, not headline. Don't drive 2.5 hours expecting steady covey flushes.

docs.title: Camping — Big Pines (the call)
docs.text:
Big Pines Recreation Area Campground (BLM, Hwy 821, milepost 10): * 42 sites — BLM's largest in the Yakima Canyon * Right on the Yakima River — true riverside camping * $15/night, $5 day use * Reservable May 1 – Sept 30; FCFS Oct 1 – April 30 — meaning the entire core fall hunting season is FCFS, no reservation gauntlet * Vault toilets, fire rings (BLM-approved metal only), picnic tables * No potable water, no hookups — bring your own water * Non-motorized river put-in/takeout at the campground * 14-day stay limit

Alternative canyon camps along Hwy 821 (all BLM, all on the river): * Umtanum Recreation Site — smaller, closer to the Umtanum Creek footbridge (the actual hunting access). Day-use leaning but overnight allowed. * Lmuma Creek Recreation Site — smaller still, quieter * Roza Recreation Site — closer to Yakima end of canyon

Why Big Pines wins: size (more chance of available sites even FCFS), real campground feel, and milepost 10 puts you central in the canyon — short drive to Umtanum trailhead for morning hunt, short drive to other access points.

docs.title: What about Yakima Sportsman State Park?
docs.text: Don't bother for the quail hunt. It closes Oct 1 through April 16 for the winter — that's the entire WA quail season. Yakima Sportsman is a summer (Apr 17 – Sept 30) camping option only. Useless for fall bird hunting trips. For quail-season camping, BLM canyon sites + Wenas dispersed are your real options.

docs.title: Big Pines vs Wenas Dispersed — Head-to-Head (the real decision)
docs.text: For a multi-day quail hunt with a 26' trailer, these are the two real contenders. The choice hinges on one question: do you want a fishing day in the mix?

docs.title: Big Pines (BLM canyon, riverside)
docs.text:
Pros * Established campground — vault toilets, fire rings, picnic tables, dumpsters * Yakima River at your feet for afternoon fishing (C&R blue-ribbon trout) — the real differentiator * $15/night, 42 sites, FCFS in fall * Hwy 821 is paved — easy trailer haul in * Neighbors-but-managed; help nearby if rig has problems

Cons * 26' trailer fit isn't guaranteed at every site — verify with BLM (509-665-2100) about specific sites before committing * You're hunting one drainage (Umtanum Creek) from this camp — risk of repetition over 3–5 days * No hookups, no potable water * Canyon walls limit sky if astronomy is in the mix * ~15 min drive + footbridge crossing to start the actual Umtanum hunt — not "step out and hunt"

docs.title: Wenas Wildlife Area dispersed (drive in to the plateau)
docs.text:
Pros * Multiple hunt units — Wenas Rd, Cleman Mountain, Audubon flats — different terrain each day, no repetition over 5 days * Step out and hunt — pick a pullout near quail habitat, no driving to trailhead * 26' fits comfortably on Wenas Rd pullouts * Free (just Discover Pass) * Privacy, no neighbors close * Higher elevation = darker sky for the Dob * No reservation system to navigate

Cons * True primitive: no toilets, water, trash, possibly no fire rings. Full self-contained required. * Wenas Rd is gravel — 26'-friendly but variable; storms or trucks can rough it up * No fishing combo — you give up the Yakima River * Cell coverage spotty * No backup if rig has problems * Fire restrictions vary; bring no-burn cooking options

docs.title: Decision rule
docs.text:
• Fishing day matters → Big Pines. Budget 2 hunt mornings + 2 fishing afternoons.
  • Pure hunt trip, more variety per day → Wenas dispersed. Multi-unit hunting over 3–5 days.
  • First-ever trip to the area, 26' trailer → Big Pines as the lower-risk learning curve; save Wenas dispersed for trip #2 once you know the terrain.

docs.title: The Umtanum Creek Trail (the actual hunt)
docs.text:
• Access: Park at Umtanum Recreation Site on Hwy 821 (~milepost 16.5). Footbridge over the Yakima River; trail begins on the west side.
  • The hunt: Trail follows Umtanum Creek up through shrub-steppe and riparian cover. Quail hold in the brushy creek margins and where sage meets riparian. Work both sides of the creek; cover-edge concentrations are where the birds are.
  • Higher up: As the trail climbs, terrain transitions to dry rocky slopes — that's chukar/Hun country. Steeper, harder hunting.

docs.title: Yakima Canyon habitat layers
docs.text:
• Canyon floor / riparian: California quail, mule deer at dawn/dusk
  • Mid-slope shrub-steppe: Hun partridge, more quail, gray partridge
  • Upper rocky slopes / rimrock: Chukar
  • Bighorn sheep visible on the canyon walls — protected, not hunted; a feature of the place

docs.title: Combo: Yakima River Trout (C&R)
docs.text:
• World-class blue-ribbon water for rainbow + cutthroat
  • Selective gear, catch-and-release only for trout
  • Access at any BLM site (Big Pines, Umtanum, Lmuma, Roza)
  • Best months: April–October for trout; fall (Sept–Oct) overlaps perfectly with quail season

docs.title: ⚠ Current Population Status (2025–26)
docs.text:
Per WDFW District 8 Hunting Prospects (Aug 2025):

"Most of the quail habitat in the Wenas Wildlife Area has burned in recent years."

2024 Black Canyon Fire burned >10,000 acres in GMUs 340 (Manastash) and 342 (Umtanum). Quail recovery is multi-year. District 8 quail harvest has been at historic lows since 2021.

For 2026 quail-focused trips, WDFW recommends moving to: 1. Yakama Nation lower Yakima River (tribal permits — 509-865-5121 x6307; Jan 1–15 extended season w/ 10-bird limit is the prize) 2. Columbia Basin (Quincy + Desert Wildlife Areas, Grant County) — #2 quail county statewide, fire-unaffected

Chukar prospects on the rocky upper Wenas may still be reasonable (less burn-vulnerable habitat); see chukar/partridge sections of the District 8 prospects for current intel.

docs.title: Dogless Hunting Note
docs.text:
Wenas is the preferred WA destination for pure dogless chukar/quail hunting vs alternatives like the Methow Wildlife Area:

  • Higher chukar density in classic rimrock-and-cheatgrass terrain — and the steep rocky country is where dogs add the least value anyway.
  • Open shrub-steppe makes downed-bird recovery realistic without a retriever.
  • Quail concentrate at water/cover edges that are mappable in advance.
  • Closer drive from Shoreline (~2.5–3 hrs) than Methow (~4–5 hrs).
  • Methow has the species-diversity edge (forest grouse, Hun partridge) but for pure dogless chukar/quail focus, drive here.

docs.title: North Cascades / Highway 20 Corridor Overview
docs.text:
• Primary Passes: Northwest Forest Pass (USFS trailheads), no fee inside North Cascades NP proper (but a WA fishing license is still required for keeping fish).
  • Key Targets: Westslope Cutthroat dominate the alpine lakes — many were stocked decades ago and now self-sustain. Some rainbow and brook in select waters.
  • Seasonality — the two-stage gate:
    1. Hwy 20 reopens typically late April or May (earliest on record: 3/10/2005; latest: 6/14/1974; recent norm has been May). Closes between mileposts 130 and 177 from ~Thanksgiving on.
    2. Lake ice-out lags the road by weeks. Alpine lakes in the 4,800–5,000+ ft band (Rainy, Cutthroat, Wing, Ann, etc.) typically clear ice late June through July, depending on snowpack year. Trails at this elevation can hold snow well into June even after the highway is open.
  • Practical fishing window: Mid-July through September is the safe bet for these lakes. May/June trips are scenic but you may be looking at ice + snow-bound trails. Higher cirques (Hidden Lake at 5,733 ft) skew later — often not fishable until July.
  • Land Mosaic: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF (west), North Cascades NP / Ross Lake NRA (middle), Okanogan-Wenatchee NF (east). Pass and rule details vary by which side of the boundary you're on — verify per-trailhead.
  • Camping in NP: Backcountry camping inside North Cascades NP requires a permit from the Marblemount ranger station; bear canisters required in many zones.

docs.title: Cutthroat Lake
docs.text:
Cutthroat Lake sits at 4,935 ft in a granite cirque directly below Cutthroat Peak, named generations ago for the fish that pack it. The approach is a friendly 2 miles and 500 ft of gain on a well-built but unpaved trail — gentle enough that it's family territory in midsummer. The basin opens up at the lake with broad shoreline on the south side, plenty of clear casting lanes, and a wide-angle view back to Cutthroat Peak's east face. The trail continues past the lake and climbs to Cutthroat Pass, so this can also be the lower leg of a longer day. The fish themselves are small (~7" average Westslope) but abundant and willing — perfect for a kid's first alpine lake or for keeping a few for a pan-fry. Less crowded than Rainy because the trail isn't paved, which filters out the casual tourist traffic.

Trailhead: From Washington Pass, drive 4.4 miles east on Hwy 20 and turn left onto the signed paved spur to the Cutthroat Lake trailhead.

docs.title: Scouting Report
docs.text:
• Bank Conditions: Open shoreline at trail's end, with multiple casting spots around the lake's southern half. Trail continues past the lake toward Cutthroat Pass.
  • Fish: Abundant Westslope Cutthroat averaging ~7" — small but eager. Perfect pan-fry size; easy fly or small spinner action.
  • Pressure: Moderate. Less crowded than Rainy because the trail is unpaved.
  • Snow Caveat: At 4,935 ft, expect snow on the trail and lingering ice on the lake into late June even after Hwy 20 reopens. See Area Overview for the corridor-wide pattern; mid-July → September is the safe window.

docs.title: Hidden Lake
docs.text:
Hidden Lake is the strenuous, scenic option — a hike-first, fish-second outing for the days you want the views as much as the catch. The lake sits at 5,733 ft in a granite cirque east of the main summit, with the historic Hidden Lake Lookout (built 1931, 6,850 ft) perched on the ridge above. The trail climbs 3,300 ft over 4.5 miles, passing through forest, meadows, and finally stark alpine granite well above treeline. Snow lingers late here; the lake stays frozen into late June or early July most years, and snowfields on the trail can persist longer. Reports mention trout in the water but the species and density aren't well-documented — this is genuinely exploratory territory, and field notes you collect here would actually fill a gap.

Trailhead: From Marblemount on Hwy 20, take Cascade River Rd ~10 mi to FR 1540, then 4.5 mi rough road to the trailhead. Road is rough enough that high clearance is recommended.

docs.title: Rainy Lake
docs.text: Rainy is a 53-acre alpine lake reached by a paved, wheelchair-accessible trail off Hwy 20 at Rainy Pass — the rare Cascade lake you can visit in dress shoes. Steep cliffs rim the south shore and feed the lake with hanging-glacier meltwater and cascading waterfalls dropping hundreds of feet off the rock. The water is glacially clear; on calm days you can see cutthroat cruising 20 ft out from the observation deck. The deck itself is the main and possibly only easy bank-access point — WDFW explicitly recommends bringing a float tube to fish the rest of the lake, where the action is. Foot traffic is heavy in midsummer because the trail is so accessible, so dawn and the shoulder season are when this lake is best. The cutthroat run a respectable 10–11", noticeably larger than most Hwy 20 alpine fish — worth the trip even just from the deck.

docs.title: Saltwater Overview
docs.text: Puget Sound shore fishing is the year-round complement to the alpine lake season — when the high country is locked under snow, the pier and beach fishery is at its best (squid in winter, lingcod in late spring, salmon in late summer/fall).

docs.title: The Marine Area System
docs.text:
WA divides marine waters into numbered Marine Areas (MAs), each with its own seasons and limits. Rules vary dramatically between adjacent MAs — what's open in MA 8-1 may be closed across a small channel in MA 9.

Area Covers Manual entries MA 8-1 Deception Pass, Hope Island, Skagit Bay Deception Pass MA 9 Admiralty Inlet (includes Edmonds, Mukilteo, Port Townsend) Edmonds Pier MA 10 Seattle–Bremerton (city piers, Alki, Discovery Park) future

Always verify current rules at the WDFW regulations page before fishing — emergency rule changes happen mid-season.

docs.title: Licenses
docs.text:
• Saltwater fishing license — required for all finfish (salmon, lingcod, flounder, etc.). Combo freshwater+saltwater is the practical buy.
  • Catch Record Card — required and free for salmon, sturgeon, halibut. Record every catch immediately.
  • Shellfish/Seaweed license — required for squid, crab, clams, mussels. Separate from the finfish license. Cheap.

docs.title: Tide Awareness
docs.text:
PNW salt fishing is tide-driven. Wrong tide = no fish. Tools:

  • Edmonds tide chart (tides4fishing) — primary reference for Edmonds Pier and nearby beaches.
  • NOAA Tides & Currents — tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov for any station; Deception Pass has its own station because the currents through the pass run 6–8 knots at peak (genuinely dangerous to wade near).

docs.title: Deception Pass
docs.text: Deception Pass is one of the few spots in Washington where you can catch a hard-fighting coho salmon from the beach, no boat needed — and it's the headline shore fishery in Marine Area 8-1. Powerful tidal currents funneling through the narrow pass concentrate baitfish, which in turn concentrate everything that eats them. Coho is the primary draw (peak August–September), but in odd-numbered years pink salmon flood through in massive numbers on their return to the Skagit (next big run: 2027). Lingcod hold on the rocky structure around the points, sea-run cutthroat work the tide rips, and surfperch are taken from the beach gravel on falling tides. Be cautious near the water — currents through the pass run 6–8 knots at peak and are genuinely dangerous; fish from the beaches, not the rocks below the bridges.

  • North Beach — north side of the pass; calmer than West Beach, productive for coho and pinks.
  • Rosario Beach / Bowman Bay — quieter, good for sea-run cutthroat and surfperch when the salmon scene is crowded.

docs.title: Coho (Silver) Salmon — the primary draw
docs.text:
• Peak: August through September.
  • Retention: MA 8-1 typically allows coho retention (unlike MA 9). Verify hatchery vs wild rules and daily limits for 2026.
  • Tactics: Buzz Bombs, Pt. Wilson Darts, casting spoons (Krocodile, Kastmaster 3/4 oz), or float-and-herring on incoming tide. First and last hours of daylight are gold.

docs.title: Pink Salmon
docs.text:
• Run years: Odd-numbered. Next strong return: 2027.
  • Peak: August.
  • Tactics: Small pink Buzz Bombs, pink jigs, small pink spoons. Pinks hit aggressively on inbound tide. When they're in, they're stacked.

docs.title: Lingcod
docs.text:
• Season (MA 8-1, 2026): Verify — typically aligns with MA 9 (May 1 – June 15) but each MA is set separately each year.
  • Size: 26–36" slot in Puget Sound.
  • Limit: Check current MA 8-1 rule (typically 1/day).
  • Tactics: Cast big jigs or swim large soft plastics over rocky structure at slack tide. Lings can be taken from West Beach rocks when tide is manageable.

docs.title: Sea-run Cutthroat
docs.text:
• Best: Fall through spring.
  • Tactics: Small streamers, Buzz Bombs, or sand-shrimp on light tackle. Work the tide rips and beach edges.
  • Limit: Standard statewide saltwater rules (verify; usually no special restrictions in MA 8-1).

docs.title: Surfperch
docs.text:
• Year-round.
  • Tactics: Sand shrimp or worms on a high-low rig, cast from beach gravel. Best on falling tide.

docs.title: Edmonds Fishing Pier
docs.text: The Edmonds pier is the gold-standard public pier in central Puget Sound — free access, lit at night, ADA-compliant, rain-covered sections, a fish-cleaning station, restrooms, and parking essentially on the structure. It sits in Marine Area 9 (Admiralty Inlet) and the pier itself has its own salmon season that's more generous than the surrounding waters. Lingcod and salmon are the marquee finfish, but the pier's real cult following is for winter night squid jigging under the bright pole lights — a uniquely accessible Puget Sound experience. Tide is everything here; high slack and the flood that follows are typically the productive windows. Plan trips around the tide chart, not your schedule.

docs.title: Methow Valley Overview
docs.text:
The Methow is the trifecta region: fishing, hunting, and astronomy all in one valley, plus excellent camping. Sitting in the rain shadow of the North Cascades, the Methow gets ~250 days of sun a year and dramatically more clear nights than anywhere on the westside. It's also one of the most beautiful river valleys in the state — wide open shrub-steppe and ponderosa pine giving way to alpine peaks on the western edge.

From Shoreline, the Methow is ~4–5 hours via Hwy 20 (open ~Memorial Day through Thanksgiving) or ~5 hours via Hwy 2 + Blewett Pass year-round.

docs.title: The Trifecta
docs.text: Activity Headline destinations Fishing Patterson Lake (rainbow, kokanee, perch, bass), Pearrygin Lake (rainbow, brown, kokanee), Methow River (resident cutthroat C&R) Hunting Methow Wildlife Area — 35,300 acres of shrub-steppe and ponderosa: chukar, California quail, gray partridge, forest grouse, mourning dove, turkey, deer Astronomy Bortle 2–3 throughout the valley. Pearrygin and Patterson lakes are darker than the Winthrop town site. See Dark Sky Sites.

docs.title: The Methow Lake Circuit
docs.text:
The lowland lakes around Winthrop have distinct fisheries — best treated as a rotation rather than a "pick one" decision. Base-camp at Pearrygin and rotate through the others.

  • Pearrygin Lake — heavily stocked rainbow + brown + kokanee. The "wake up and fish from camp" lake. Easy, family-friendly, fish-from-shore.
  • Patterson Lake — diverse fishery (rainbow, kokanee, perch, both bass species). 7 mi SW of Winthrop. Different bag-of-tricks day.
  • Big Twin Lake — selective gear only (barbless, no bait). Rainbows 10–18" with occasional larger carryover. The "trophy/quality" water of the cluster; bring spinners/spoons/flies, leave the PowerBait in camp. ~15 min from Pearrygin. Winterkill events in 2016–18 dented the carryover population, so check current reports.
  • Davis & Campbell Lakes — unusual September 1 opener with April catch-and-release; otherwise closed. Useful when the standard season winds down and you're in the valley for fall hunting/astronomy.

docs.title: Seasonality
docs.text:
• Spring (Apr–May): Lake fishing wakes up — Pearrygin and Patterson start hot in late April. River trout closed (opens June 1).
  • Summer (Jun–Sep): Peak everything except hunting. Long, dry, clear nights → astronomy prime time. Lakes warm up; fish early/late. River trout open with selective gear.
  • Fall (Sep–Nov): The single best window for combo trips. Upland bird seasons open, lake fishing still productive, nights getting darker earlier (less time waiting for true astronomical twilight), aspens turn gold. Hwy 20 still open through ~Thanksgiving.
  • Winter (Dec–Mar): Pearrygin Lake SP closed Nov 1 – Mar 31. Some lakes ice-fish (Patterson). Methow Wildlife Area accessible but bring snow gear. Hwy 20 closed; reach via Blewett.

docs.title: Passes & Logistics
docs.text:
• Discover Pass — required on WDFW (Patterson, Methow Wildlife Area) AND state parks (Pearrygin). One pass covers both. Vehicle Access Pass that comes free with a hunting/fishing license can substitute on WDFW lands but not state parks.
  • No NWFP needed in the valley proper.
  • Towns: Winthrop (Old West-themed, fly shops, groceries), Twisp (smaller, year-round), Mazama (north of Winthrop, closest to Hwy 20 west access).
  • Fly shops: Methow Fishing Adventures, Mazama Store — both have current river-condition intel.

docs.title: Camping Anchor Options
docs.text:
• Pearrygin Lake State Park — developed, hookups, 4 mi NE of Winthrop (Apr–Oct only).
  • Forest Service dispersed sites along Twisp River Rd, Chewuch River Rd, Lost River Rd — free, primitive, scattered. Self-contained / Leave No Trace.
  • Methow Valley private resorts/cabins — Patterson Lake Resort has waterfront cabins.

docs.title: Notable 2026 Alerts
docs.text: • Big Valley Unit (Methow Wildlife Area) — partial closure until Sept 14, 2026 to protect nesting sandhill cranes. Verify exact closure boundaries at WDFW before hunting there.

docs.title: Methow River
docs.text:
The Methow is a beautiful, classically braided eastside river — gravel-and-cobble runs, clear cold water, riffles tailing into deep slow pools, and a season tightly bound to the snowpack year above it. For your stated style (catch-and-keep), the Methow is more of a "fish if you're there for other reasons" river than a destination. Most current rules favor catch-and-release with selective gear. Anadromous fisheries (steelhead, salmon) are heavily constrained by ESA protections; the upper Columbia steelhead and Methow spring chinook are listed and runs collapsed years ago. Some hatchery-only steelhead seasons have reopened in recent years on a year-by-year basis. Resident cutthroat fishing opens June 1 under selective gear rules — barbless single hooks, no bait — and is fun on a fly rod or small spinning gear, but it's not catch-and-keep water.

Bottom line: treat the Methow as a scenic supplement to your lake fishing, not the main event. Verify current 2026 regs at WDFW before fishing — the rules change.

docs.title: Methow Wildlife Area
docs.text: The Methow Wildlife Area is the headline upland bird destination in WA within a weekend's drive of Seattle — roughly 35,300 acres spanning the lower Methow River drainage in western Okanogan County. The habitat mosaic is textbook upland: shrub-steppe and sage flats on the lower benches, transitioning to grassland and dry ponderosa pine on the mid-slopes, with rocky rimrock canyons cutting through. That mix supports nearly every WA upland bird species in one area — chukar in the rocky steeps, quail in the sage and water-edge cover, gray partridge in the agricultural fringe, forest grouse in the pine, plus mourning dove and turkey. Big game (mule deer, black bear, occasional cougar) is incidental but real. The area is broken into multiple management units — Big Buck, Big Valley, Methow Unit, Texas Creek — each with slightly different access roads and use patterns. Discover Pass required (or Vehicle Access Pass from a hunting/fishing license purchase).

    • California Quail: brushy riparian fringe, agricultural edges, water-and-cover transitions.
    • Gray Partridge: open grassland and agricultural fringe — flat, walkable hunting.
    • Forest Grouse (Ruffed, Dusky/Blue, Spruce): higher-elevation timber and forest edges.
    • Mourning Dove: Sept opener; sit water and gravel roads in the early morning.
    • Turkey: Spring and fall seasons; forest edges and meadow margins.
  • Vehicle / Trailer Access: Multiple gravel/forest road systems accessing each unit. Most accommodate 2WD in dry conditions; some unit access roads get rough.
  • Hunt-with-dog factor: This is dog country — long walks across open terrain, classic pointer / flusher work. For pure dogless chukar/quail hunting, Wenas is denser and easier; Methow's edge is species diversity and the trifecta-trip combo, not raw bird density per mile walked.

docs.title: Patterson Lake
docs.text: Patterson is the western Methow Valley's classic year-round lake — small enough to feel intimate, productive enough to draw anglers in every season including winter ice fishery. Just west of Winthrop, set in dry pine and open meadow, it's the kind of place where the trifecta of fishing in the morning, hiking the Methow Trails network in the afternoon, and rolling out the Dobsonian after sunset works seamlessly. Unlike most WA lakes it holds a real diversity of fish — rainbow trout are the headline, but kokanee, yellow perch, and both bass species share the water. WDFW maintains a gravel boat launch on the west side; the east shore is dominated by Patterson Lake Resort with rental cabins and small boats. Discover Pass required for the WDFW access.

  • Ice fishery: Increasingly popular winter target — trout, kokanee, and perch all caught through the ice.

docs.title: Pearrygin Lake State Park
docs.text: Pearrygin is the gold-standard developed-camping anchor for any Methow Valley trip — 1,186 acres of state park wrapped around 11,000 ft of shoreline on a spring-fed lake just four miles northeast of Winthrop. The park has 153 campsites across two areas (76 standard, 50 full hookup, 27 partial hookup), a boat launch, a swim beach, and 3 miles of trail. The water is genuinely good for trout (stocked rainbows averaging 10–13" with carryover fish to 15"+, plus brown trout and kokanee), and the surrounding land transitions from sage flat to ponderosa benches with sharp peaks visible to the west. Set up camp here, fish at dawn, hunt the Methow Wildlife Area in the morning, and you've got the Dobsonian out by 10 PM — that's the Methow combo trip in a sentence.

docs.title: Salmon La Sac / Cle Elum / Teanaway Overview
docs.text:
The closest serious eastside combo region from Shoreline — ~2.5 hours via I-90 + Hwy 970 to the Cle Elum / Roslyn / Salmon La Sac area, vs ~4–5 hours to Methow. Trades some Methow advantages (darker skies, denser bird hunting) for proximity. Centered on the Cle Elum River drainage as it climbs from Cle Elum Lake (reservoir) up through Salmon La Sac into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, plus the Teanaway River valley to the east.

The terrain mix is classic Cascade east-slope transition: dry ponderosa lower down, dense hemlock/fir mid-slope, granite alpine at the top. Long sunny days, big peaks visible from camp, manageable drive.

docs.title: The Combo at a Glance
docs.text: Activity Headline destinations Drive-to lake fishing Cooper Lake (rainbow, brook, brown, kokanee, cutthroat), Cle Elum Lake reservoir (kokanee 9–15", smallmouth) Hike-in lake fishing Pete Lake (~4 mi easy, brook trout) — and longer options like Spectacle and Waptus from the same trailhead system River fishing Cle Elum River — catch-and-release for cutthroat and rainbow under selective gear (year-round on the lower reach). Real fishery for fly-rod release fishing. Hunting / hiking / camping Teanaway Community Forest — 50,272 acres DNR/WDFW jointly managed. Mule deer, forest grouse, hiking, designated camping (no dispersed). Astronomy Bortle ~3 — not as dark as Methow but the drive is half. Reasonable combo target on clear nights.

docs.title: Seasonality
docs.text:
• Spring (Apr–May): Lake ice goes out at Cooper by mid-April; Pete and the higher alpine lakes hold ice into late May. Salmon La Sac Campground closed until ~May. Cle Elum River selective-gear/C&R already in effect.
  • Summer (Jun–Sep): Peak window. All lakes fishable, hike-in trails open, hunting closed but everything else firing. Hot midday on the dry side; fish/scope at dawn and dusk.
  • Fall (Sep–Oct): Best combo trip window — bird seasons opening, lake fishing still solid, larch turning gold in late September, nights cooling down for astronomy. Salmon La Sac Campground closes after October.
  • Winter (Nov–Mar): Salmon La Sac closed. Cooper Lake fishable year-round but you're battling snow on Cle Elum River Rd. Cle Elum River selective gear (with whitefish gear allowed Dec 1 – end of Feb) for those who want to suffer for fish.

docs.title: Passes & Logistics
docs.text:
• Northwest Forest Pass — required at Cooper Lake / Pete Lake trailheads and Salmon La Sac area
  • Discover Pass — required on Teanaway Community Forest (DNR land)
  • Towns: Cle Elum (groceries, gas, Pioneer Coffee), Roslyn (small but charming — Northern Exposure filming location), Easton (smaller still, gateway to lake area)
  • Fly shop: Cle Elum's local tackle is limited; closest serious fly shop is Worley Bugger Fly Co. in Ellensburg (35 min south) — they know the Cle Elum / Yakima drainages well.

docs.title: Camping Anchor Options
docs.text:
• Salmon La Sac Campground (USFS, developed) — 67 sites, 40 reservable. Closed October–April. Near Cle Elum River.
  • Owhi Campground at Cooper Lake (USFS) — 22 walk-in tent-only sites, basic facilities. NWFP required.
  • Cle Elum River Rd dispersed sites (USFS) — primitive pullouts along the road north of the developed campgrounds. Self-contained, Leave No Trace.
  • Teanaway Community Forest designated campgrounds — no dispersed camping allowed. Use 29 Pines, Teanaway, or Indian Camp (see Teanaway page).

docs.title: Notable 2026 Alerts
docs.text:
• 29 Pines Campground (Teanaway) — closed for flood-damage repair. Verify status with DNR before planning around it; extensive damage may impact even neighboring sites.
  • West Teanaway Trailhead and West Fork Trails opening June 6, 2026 — new access opens up additional Teanaway hiking.

docs.title: Cle Elum vs Methow — picking between them
docs.text:
Both are eastside combo regions. Rule of thumb:

  • Choose Cle Elum/Salmon La Sac for: shorter drive, more developed-camping options, year-round lake fishing (Cooper), shoulder-season trips.
  • Choose Methow for: darker skies (astronomy), denser upland bird hunting, longer/wilder feel, when you want a 3–4 day base camp instead of a 2-day visit.

docs.title: Cle Elum River
docs.text: The Cle Elum is one of the central Cascades' great fly-rod rivers — a clear, cobble-bottomed freestone that drains the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, runs through Cle Elum Lake (the reservoir), and joins the Yakima at the town of Cle Elum. For trout, it's a catch-and-release fishery under selective-gear rules; if you're looking for keeper fish, you'll find them in Cooper Lake or Cle Elum Lake's kokanee, not here. The river holds all four major salmonid species — wild rainbow, native cutthroat, ESA-listed bull trout, and kokanee — plus mountain whitefish that are open to retention under statewide rules and are actually a legitimate eat in winter. The lower reach (mouth to Cle Elum Dam) is open year-round with selective gear, with a special winter window allowing whitefish gear. The upper reach above the lake (up to Hyas Lake outlet) is open Saturday before Memorial Day through October 31, also selective gear.

docs.title: Lower reach — from mouth to Cle Elum Dam
docs.text: All species: It is permissible to fish up to the base of Cle Elum Dam. Mar. 1 – Nov. 30: Selective gear rules. Dec. 1 – Last Day of Feb.: Selective gear rules except whitefish gear may be used. Trout (year-round): Statewide min. size/daily limit. Except: Release cutthroat trout and rainbow trout. Other game fish (year-round): Statewide min. size/daily limit.

docs.text: All species: Selective gear rules. All game fish: Sat. before Memorial Day – Oct. 31. Statewide min. size/daily limit.

docs.title: What "Selective Gear Rules" actually means
docs.text:
• Single-point barbless hooks only
  • No bait of any kind (no PowerBait, Mice Tails, Trout Worms, Power Eggs, sand shrimp, salmon eggs, worms)
  • Artificial flies and lures only

docs.title: Bull Trout
docs.text:
• Present throughout the Cle Elum drainage; catch-and-release statewide, ESA-listed
  • ID: white-edged dorsal/anal/pelvic fins, no black spots on dorsal fin
  • When in doubt → release

docs.title: Why fish a C&R river?
docs.text:
• Wild fish quality — Cle Elum cutthroat and rainbow are educated, beautiful, and well-conditioned
  • Drift presentation practice that pays off elsewhere
  • The river itself is a gorgeous place to spend a half-day
  • Mountain whitefish are retainable and are actually excellent smoked — don't sleep on this in winter

docs.title: Tackle
docs.text:
✅ Will work: * Inline spinners (Rooster Tails, Mepps Aglia #0–#1, Panther Martin) with trebles crushed barbless OR replaced with single siwash hooks * Small spoons (Kastmaster 1/12–1/8 oz, Little Cleo) — same hook conversion * Bubble + fly rig with small dries (Parachute Adams, Elk Hair Caddis) or wets (soft hackles, small streamers, small nymphs) * Existing Fenwick 6.5' Light + Okuma 2500 + 4 lb fluoro leader = right setup

❌ Leave in the car: * All scented baits — PowerBait, Power Eggs, Mice Tails, Trout Worms * Gulp! / Berkley scented soft plastics * Sand shrimp, salmon eggs, worms * Treble hooks unless converted to single barbless

docs.title: Cooper Lake
docs.text: Cooper Lake is the drive-to anchor of the Salmon La Sac fishery — a quiet 120-acre lake 3.5 miles northwest of Salmon La Sac up the Cooper River drainage, ringed by old-growth conifers and rimmed by granite peaks on the north side. The fishery is unusually diverse for an alpine-foothill lake: rainbow and eastern brook trout in the 8–10" range, plus brown trout running 1–3 lbs (occasionally larger), small kokanee, and the occasional cutthroat. Bull trout are present and must be released — they're ESA-listed and Cooper Lake is specifically closed to bull trout retention. The lake is open year-round, which makes it one of the few productive eastside fisheries you can hit in winter (snow road conditions permitting). A USFS boat launch sits near Owhi Campground on the north shore, but a county ordinance prohibits all motors — so you're paddling, rowing, or float-tubing.

docs.title: Scouting Report
docs.text:
• Bank Conditions: Shore access is okay near the boat launch and around Owhi Campground; much of the rest is brushy or steep. A float tube transforms productivity here.
  • Fish: Rainbows and brook (8–10") are the day-to-day catch. Brown trout to 3+ lbs are the trophy class — fish them deeper and slower. Kokanee small but present.
  • Bull Trout ID: White-edged dorsal/anal/pelvic fins, no black spots on dorsal — release immediately, don't lift from water if possible.
  • Approach: Cle Elum River Rd (Hwy 903) north to FR 46, then FR 4616 to the lake. Last 1+ miles are gravel; passable in 2WD when dry.

docs.title: Field Notes
docs.text: • Track what each species took — Cooper is the lake where pattern-by-species notes really pay off given the diversity.

docs.title: Pete Lake
docs.text: Pete Lake is the quintessential easy-hike-in alpine trout lake — 4 miles of nearly-flat trail following the Cooper River through old-growth Douglas fir and western hemlock to a long lake sitting in the shadow of Big Summit Chief and Chimney Rock. The trail's gentle grade makes it accessible for families and first-time backpackers; pack animals and equestrians share it. The fishery is eastern brook trout of varying sizes — the shoreline is shallow over much of the lake, which makes shore casting more work than usual, but the brookies are willing and the place is genuinely beautiful. Backcountry campsites at the lake fill up on summer weekends; midweek and shoulder seasons are golden. Early-season water crossings on the trail can be tricky for kids.

docs.text:
Open in Google Maps →

docs.title: Scouting Report
docs.text:
• Bank Conditions: Long shoreline but much of it is shallow with submerged structure. Best shore-casting is from the inlet and outlet ends and at a few small clearings around the perimeter; bring polarized sunglasses to sight-fish cruising brookies. A packable float tube would punch above its weight here.
  • Fish: Eastern brook trout, varying sizes — typical alpine fish are 8–12" but bigger holdovers exist. Stocked over the years; now reproducing.
  • Trail Approach: From Cooper Lake trailhead area (off FR 46 then FR 4616), 4 miles one-way, ~400 ft gain. Gentle. Equestrian and pack-stock traffic on busy days.
  • Continuing past Pete: Spectacle Lake is another 2.5 miles further up; the PCT crosses just past Pete Lake. A bigger day or overnight option.

docs.text: • Track which end of the lake produced and what depth (sight-fishing notes helpful). Bring repellent — Pete Lake is famously buggy in early summer.

docs.title: Teanaway Community Forest
docs.text:
The Teanaway is a 50,272-acre dual-use working/recreation forest in the central Cascades just north of Cle Elum — Washington's first state-owned community forest, acquired by DNR in 2013. It's jointly managed by DNR and WDFW with significant community-board input, which gives it a different feel from purely-USFS lands: more designated infrastructure, more rules, less freelancing. About 47 miles of groomed trails, three designated campgrounds, and a mosaic of meadow / ponderosa pine / dry conifer habitat across the Teanaway River drainage.

The headline difference from typical USFS dispersed-camping country: no dispersed camping allowed. Camping is restricted to the three designated campgrounds. That's the trade-off for the protected status and trail investment. Hunting and fishing are open under standard WDFW regulations.

docs.title: Hunting
docs.text:
• Mule Deer: Primary big-game target. Modern firearm general season plus archery and muzzleloader windows — verify current WDFW hunt regulations and unit boundaries.
  • Forest Grouse: Ruffed and dusky/blue grouse along forest edges and meadow margins. Walking forest roads at dawn is the move.
  • Note: This is not classic upland chukar/quail country like the Methow — it's a forested-mid-elevation hunt. Different style.

docs.title: Fishing
docs.text: • Teanaway River and tributaries hold rainbow and cutthroat. Verify per-stream rules in the WDFW pamphlet — most central-WA streams are selective gear with restrictive trout retention.

docs.title: Columbia Basin Overview
docs.text:
The Columbia Basin — Grant and Adams counties in central Washington — is the actual best fall quail destination within driving range of Shoreline as of 2026. This region exists in the manual because the original "Yakima Canyon / Wenas" plan turned out to be a poor fit for current quail populations (see Umtanum/Yakima Canyon page for that reality check). The Columbia Basin is the corrected answer.

Why here: - WDFW: "California quail continue to be the most abundant and popular upland game birds in District 5. Grant County is one of the top-producing counties." - Fire-unaffected habitat unlike the Wenas/Umtanum complex (Black Canyon Fire 2024) - Agricultural / CRP / irrigation-ditch habitat — exactly the "near rivers and irrigated land" the WDFW biologist flagged as the productive cover type - ~3 hours from Shoreline via I-90 East — similar drive to Methow, shorter than most eastside options - Bonus species mix: pheasant, chukar, Hungarian partridge, mourning dove (early season), waterfowl on the seep lakes - Fishing combo: Potholes Reservoir is a serious walleye/bass/perch fishery right at the Potholes SP camp; the Desert WA seep-lake chain holds stocked trout and warmwater species; Lenice/Nunnally to the east are quality trout water. See the Desert WA page for details.

docs.title: WA Quail Geography (Historic + Current)
docs.text:
Yakima and Grant counties consistently yield the highest quail harvests in the state. Different intel sources triangulate on the same three productive cover types:

  • Russian olive thickets — dense brushy cover near water; California quail magnets
  • Irrigation sloughs — water + cover at the ag fringe
  • Riparian edges near agricultural land — the transition where wet meets dry meets crop

Current calibration (post-2024 fires): Yakima County (Wenas Wildlife Area) is historically #1 but the 2024 Black Canyon Fire burned 10,000+ acres in GMUs 340 & 342, including much of the Wenas quail habitat. For 2026, Grant County (Desert WA, Lower Crab Creek, Gloyd Seeps, Upland Restoration parcels) is the practical primary. See the Yakima/Wenas Region for the historic context and Umtanum/Yakima Canyon for the reality-check on that recovery.

docs.title: The Two Headline Wildlife Areas
docs.text:
Area Acres Trailer access in quail season Best for Quincy Lakes Unit Part of 160,100-acre Columbia Basin WA ⚠ Main access road CLOSED Oct 1 – Mar 1 to vehicles; foot only Walk-in quail / pheasant; park on perimeter Desert Wildlife Area 35,100 (Grant Co.) Open during quail season Better trailer fit. Mixed habitat: quail, pheasant, chukar, Hun

For a 26' trailer + fall hunt, Desert Wildlife Area is the better primary base. Quincy is still worth hunting on foot from a perimeter park, but you don't drive your rig into it during the season.

docs.title: Fall Weather Expectations (Moses Lake / Columbia Basin)
docs.text:
Eastside continental climate — cool, mostly dry, and windier than the westside because the open shrub-steppe has no tree cover. Plan layered clothing and bring wind protection.

Month Typical highs Typical lows Conditions October 73 → 56°F (declines through month) 50 → 38°F Mild, mostly dry early; cloudier and cooler late month. First frost mid-to-late October. November ~50 → 40°F 30s Frosts regular; first snow possible. Increasing fog days. December 34°F avg high 24°F avg low Snow normal (~2.6" total, falls ~7 days/month). Coldest, foggiest. Wind Year-round factor in the Basin Average ~6 mph in winter; gusts higher. Wind shell mandatory. Precip ~1" per month in late fall Dry overall vs westside; the cold is the bigger issue than the wet.

docs.title: Practical implications
docs.text:
• Layers, not single heavy: big swings between dawn (cold) and midday (warmer) — fleece + wind shell + insulated outer
  • Trailer water management: by mid-November you're getting overnight freezes regularly. Drain hose between uses; consider heated hose if you'll be there in December
  • Hunting: cold birds hold tighter at dawn; midday warming gets them moving; wind makes flushing distances longer
  • Fishing: water temps dropping = walleye go deeper but feed actively; trout in seep lakes get slower; bass shut down by mid-November
  • Hookup heat: electric heat at camp is the whole point of hookups for fall trips — no apology needed

docs.title: Season & Limits
docs.text:
• WA Eastern California (Valley) Quail season: Oct 4 – Jan 19 (2025–26)
  • Daily limit: 10 mixed bag (all quail species combined)
  • Possession limit: 30
  • Bonus seasons may overlap: pheasant (Oct–Jan), chukar/Hun partridge (Oct–Jan), mourning dove (Sept–Oct opener)
  • Always verify exact dates in the current WDFW Game Bird pamphlet.

docs.title: Additional Areas Worth Knowing
docs.text: Beyond the two headline units, the broader Columbia Basin hunting landscape includes:

docs.title: Quail hotspots (per Columbia Basin intel — multiple sources agree)
docs.text:
• Lower Crab Creek (Lower Crab Creek Wildlife Area Unit) — east of Desert WA, between Corfu and the Columbia River. Confirmed quail hotspot in addition to its known trout fishery (Lenice, Nunnally).
  • Desert Wildlife Area — covered in detail on its own page; #1 confirmed quail spot in this region for your trip.
  • Gloyd Seeps — between Stratford and Moses Lake. WDFW unit; riparian/seep habitat, lower-pressure than the headline units. "If Quincy/Desert are crowded, drive 20 min north" option.
  • Upland Restoration Unit (Columbia Basin Wildlife Area) — specifically managed for upland habitat restoration = quail/pheasant by design. Multiple scattered properties:
    • 6 properties between Quincy and Ephrata off Hwy 28 W
    • 2 properties within 12 mi SE of Moses Lake (off Road N NE, and N of I-90 west of Road U NE) — close to Potholes SP base
    • 11 properties within 2-7 mi around Warden + 2 in Adams County
    • 1 property 4 mi NE of Royal City off Road 11.2 SW
    • ⚠ "Public access is limited" per WDFW — verify each parcel via OnX/Gaia + WDFW before driving in. Some are walk-only, some have specific access points.
    • The Moses Lake-area parcels are worth checking as alternate scouting from your Potholes SP base.
  • Potholes Reservoir Unit (waterfowl-mixed) — adjacent to Desert WA; mixed waterfowl + upland; covered separately as a fishing destination on Potholes Reservoir

docs.title: Chukar corridor (per same older Columbia Basin intel)
docs.text:
• Coulee scabland corridor — Lake Lenore up to south end of Banks Lake. This is the named chukar destination in the broader Basin per old hunter wisdom. Coulee scabland = rocky steep terrain = classic chukar country, matches the typical "rocky breaks + cheatgrass" pattern. North of the Desert WA / Potholes zone; would be a separate trip orientation.
  • Columbia River breaks north of Vantage — second chukar option; steep, classic dogless terrain.

docs.title: Other named units
docs.text:
• Dry Falls unit — south end of Banks Lake.
  • Royal Slope (Hunt by Reservation Program) — structured permit-only access; submit application via WDFW if interested.

docs.title: Dogless Tactics That Apply Here
docs.text:
• Plan to hit multiple coveys, not one. Per local intel: "Large coveys are difficult to find by mid-season on public lands" — successful hunters identify multiple spots and rotate.
  • Lean on riparian zones — water-and-cover edges are still the highest-percentage starting point, exactly the dogless-friendly mappable terrain
  • Remote shrub cover away from pressure holds the birds that walked away from the road; willing to walk = willing to find
  • Honest caveat: the local 2015 hunting prospects article explicitly says dogs significantly improve quail success. Going dogless here is doable but you're playing on harder mode — lean even harder on terrain, water, and timing.

docs.title: Columbia Basin Camping for a 26' Trailer with Hookups
docs.text: For fall hunts (Oct–Dec), hookups are the right call — temperatures drop steeply at dusk, electric heat is welcome, and there's no penalty for being civilized. All recommended options below are open during the full fall quail season unless noted.

docs.title: Geographic Reality First
docs.text:
The two huntable areas are on opposite sides of the Columbia Basin:

Hunt Area Location Closest hookup town Drive between areas Desert Wildlife Area West of Moses Lake Moses Lake (Potholes SP, etc.) — Quincy Lakes WA Unit (part of Columbia Basin WA) West of George / near Vantage Vantage / Quincy ~50 min between areas

Pick one primary hunt area and camp near it. Don't try to base near both. Quincy Lakes is walk-in only during quail season (Oct 1 – Mar 1 road closure inside the unit), and Desert WA is the bigger / more diverse / vehicle-accessible option — making Desert WA the strong default primary.

docs.text:

docs.title: Middle-Ground Option (if you really want to hit both areas)
Ephrata RV Park (private, full hookups, central Grant Co.)
docs.text:
• Location: Ephrata, central Grant County
  • Distance to Quincy Lakes WA: ~20–25 min
  • Distance to Desert WA: ~30 min
  • Sites: Big-rig friendly 30/50 amp full hookup pull-throughs
  • Season: Year-round

docs.title: Decision Rule
docs.text:
• Desert WA focus (primary recommendation) + hookup priority → Potholes SP (reserve early), Mar Don Resort backup
  • Quincy Lakes focus + hookups → Vantage Riverstone Resort or Crescent Bar Recreation Area
  • Want to hunt both areas from one camp → Ephrata RV Park (longer drives but central)
  • Best resupply / restaurants → Suncrest RV or Mar Don Resort
  • Cheapest hookup → Cascade Campground

docs.title: Booking Note
docs.text: Reservable state parks (Potholes SP) need advance booking even for fall. Mid-week is your friend. Call private RV parks directly — they typically have more availability and aren't gamed by booking bots like the state-park system.

docs.title: Desert Wildlife Area Unit
docs.text:
62,601 acres in Grant County, southwest of Moses Lake, west of Potholes Reservoir, and south of Interstate 90. Within the Lower Crab Creek watershed. Game Management Units 278 and 290. Mixed shrubsteppe / wetlands / ponds / desert upland habitat. Managed by WDFW with portions transferred via Memorandum of Understanding with the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation. Unlike Quincy Lakes Unit, there's no seasonal vehicle access closure — you can drive in to hunt during the entire quail season.

Note on naming: the Winchester Game Reserve (closed to hunting, see below) is within Desert WA south of I-90. Winchester Wasteway / Winchester Reservoir as map features are north of I-90 — different geographic context despite the shared "Winchester" name. Verify exact reserve boundaries on the WDFW map before relying on this distinction.

Highlighted wildlife on WDFW unit page: mule deer and American white pelican. The huntable game-bird species (pheasant, chukar, Hungarian partridge, quail) are confirmed in the broader District 5 hunting prospects — Grant County is one of the top quail-producing counties in WA — but the WDFW unit page itself emphasizes broader wildlife rather than calling out quail specifically.

WDFW explicitly lists pheasant, chukar, Hungarian partridge, and quail as huntable species. Grant County is one of the top quail-producing counties in WA, and District 5 biologists call California quail the most abundant and popular upland game bird in the district. This is real, current bird country, not a recovering burn zone.

docs.title: ⚠ Non-Toxic Shot — REQUIRED
docs.text:
Lead shot is illegal at Desert WA. Per WDFW verbatim:

"Non-toxic shot is required for hunting all game birds and game animals in the Columbia Basin Wildlife Area (which includes the Banks Lake, Gloyd Seeps, Lower Crab Creek, Quincy Lakes, and Warden units)."

Desert Unit is part of the Columbia Basin Wildlife Area Complex — the rule applies here.

Penalty: mandatory $1,000 fine + 2-year loss of small game hunting privileges. This is the kind of rule that gets enforced — bring only non-toxic ammo.

docs.title: Non-toxic ammo options for upland (12g and 20g)
docs.text:
• Steel — cheapest non-toxic option; $20–30/box of 25
    • Patterns tighter than lead; go one shot size larger than your lead-equivalent
    • For quail: #6 or #7 steel (vs #7.5 lead)
    • For pheasant: #4 or #5 steel
    • Modified or tighter chokes with steel risk damage on older barrels — verify your barrel is rated for steel
  • Bismuth — softest, most lead-like behavior; $35–45/box (most expensive)
    • Boss Bismuth, Federal Bismuth, Rio Bismuth — premium options
    • Safe through any choke; performs nearly identical to lead
    • The choice if your gun isn't steel-rated
  • Hevi-Metal / Hevi-Bismuth blends — middle-ground performance and price ($30–35)
  • Tungsten Super Shot (TSS) — densest, highest performance; $$$ (~$50+); usually overkill for upland

docs.title: Recoil-equivalent 12g loads (mimicking 20g)
docs.text:
If you're using a 12g (rather than buying a 20g), drop payload to reduce recoil:

  • 1 oz 12g steel/bismuth #6 or #7 — recoil feels close to standard 20g
  • Avoid the standard 1 1/8 oz loads — those make 12g feel like 12g (heavier kick, more fatigue late in the day)

docs.title: Pre-trip checklist for ammo
docs.text:
• Buy non-toxic at least a week before the trip — local sporting goods can be picked over in fall
  • Pattern-test at 20 and 30 yards on a butcher-paper target before trusting the load on birds — non-toxic patterns differently than lead through the same choke
  • Keep the receipt or a photo of the box label in your hunting kit; in the unlikely event of a contact, having proof you bought non-toxic is helpful

docs.text:

  • Winchester Game Reserve
  • Frenchman Hills Game Reserve

docs.title: Terrain (per WDFW)
docs.text:
"Reservoir, sand dunes, shrubsteppe, basalt outcroppings with big sage and bluebunch wheatgrass, and some wetlands."

Sub-region breakdown (per WDFW page):

  • Western part: active sand dunes; shrubsteppe except for wetland areas along the Winchester and Frenchman Hills wasteways. Rolling, soft underfoot, not steep. Sand walking is tiring but it's not climbing.
  • Eastern part: mostly sand / gravel / round rock soil; shrubsteppe vegetation bordered by irrigated farmland. Primarily rabbitbrush and needle and thread grass. Flat to gently rolling, walkable.
  • Southern part (near O'Sullivan Dam): mostly basalt outcroppings with big sage and bluebunch wheatgrass. Rockier, mildly steeper, but not canyon country.

docs.title: Habitat Composition (detailed)
docs.text:
Much of the area is freshwater marshes, ponds, braiding channels, and small lakes. Tracts of sand dunes and shrub-steppe make up the remainder of the landmass.

Riparian habitats are located along Frenchman Hills Road and Road C SE, with several isolated stands of Russian olive and willow along the wetlands.

The shrub-steppe is composed of typical plant communities of sages, rabbitbrush, and bitterbrush interspersed with various grasses and forbs.

⚡ Quail-hunt actionable from this: * Russian olive thickets are textbook California quail magnets — they love the dense brushy cover next to water. Mark every Russian olive stand you see on satellite or in person. * Frenchman Hills Road and Road C SE are the named riparian-access roads per WDFW description — these are your two primary scouting drives for quail-productive cover. * Willow stands along the wetlands are secondary high-percentage quail spots.

Compared to Wenas/Umtanum (classic rimrock canyon country with 30–60% slopes): this is dramatically less punishing. Desert WA is walkable shrub-steppe with open visibility — good for dogless glassing-and-walking tactics, no climbing required.

To preview before committing: Google Street View along Frenchman Hills Road or Road C SE (the riparian-access roads) and Road M SW or Dodson Road. Google Earth satellite shows the Russian olive thickets as dark green clumps along the wasteway corridors — visible from above.

docs.title: Scouting Report
docs.text:
• Habitat layers:
    • Riparian and pond edges — primary quail concentration zones
    • CRP / cheatgrass / ag fringe — pheasant + quail mix
    • Sage flats and rocky breaks — chukar / Hun partridge
    • Wetlands and seep lakes — waterfowl (separate license/stamps required for ducks/geese)
  • Access roads (per WDFW): Road M SW, Frenchman Hills Road, Dodson Road, Adams Road, Fidesco-Harris Access, Road I SW
  • Vehicle access: Permitted year-round; verify any temporary fire/habitat closures via WDFW before going

docs.title: Best Access Zones (what's verified vs what isn't)
docs.text:
Verified productive corridors (per WDFW + Oregon DFW guide referencing the Desert Unit):

  • Winchester Wasteway corridor — irrigation drainage that meanders southeast across several miles of the Desert Unit before emptying into SW Potholes Reservoir. "Public lands along both Frenchman and Winchester wasteway should hold ducks" per Oregon DFW's Columbia Basin guide — and the riparian-sage edges along the wasteways are exactly the quail concentration zones WDFW District 5 calls out as the best chance for coveys.
    • Don't confuse: the Winchester Wasteway (south of I-90, in Desert WA, huntable) vs the Winchester Reservoir Wildlife Area Unit (separate WDFW unit, north of I-90) vs the Winchester Game Reserve (CLOSED to hunting — see above)
  • Frenchman Hills Wasteway corridor — parallel feature, same SE-trending irrigation drainage; similar riparian habitat. Same productivity logic.
  • Frenchman Regulated Access Area — has WDFW-planted food plots intended for waterfowl; the adjacent cover holds upland birds too.

Named riparian-access roads (per WDFW habitat description):

  • Frenchman Hills Road — one of the two named roads with riparian habitat. Drive it, walk in at promising stands.
  • Road C SE — second named riparian-access road. The wasteway / Russian olive / willow thicket cover is here.

Logical "good bet" zones (high-percentage by habitat type):

  • Russian olive thickets along the wasteways — textbook California quail magnets; visible as dark green clumps on satellite
  • Willow stands along the wetland edges — secondary high-percentage cover
  • Where any access road meets the wasteways or pond edges — riparian-sage interface is the verified quail concentration zone
  • Mid-slope transitions where sage flat meets the wasteway riparian — quail move between water and cover here at dawn/dusk
  • Brushy ditch banks along access roads — small coveys hold tight

Gap honestly flagged: I don't have specific hunter-report intel for "end of [road X]" honey holes. Field experience and a phone call to WDFW District 5 (Ephrata): (509) 754-4624 is the way to get current spot-specific intel — they'll talk to hunters and have a sense of where birds are this season.

  • Frenchman Hills Game Reserve (within Desert WA) — same

These are distinct from the wasteways of the same name. Mark exact boundaries on GPS before hunting — trespass into a closed reserve is a citable offense regardless of intent.

docs.text: 27,800-acre reservoir 5 mi south of Moses Lake. WA's marquee walleye fishery + a serious panfish destination. 22 species per WDFW. Camp at Potholes State Park for full-hookup lakeside base. The adjacent hunting unit (Desert Wildlife Area) is a separate trip type — this page is the fishing standalone.

docs.text:
Trip type Target Rig Why Spring/early-summer couple trip Bluegill / panfish from shore Both rigs ideal — Shakespeare 5.5' shines for tight-bank casting June = spawning peak; fish stacked at shoreline; easy + productive Stocked trout day Rainbow trout in Desert WA seep lakes Sliding-sinker dough rig 15–20 min drive from camp; predictable success Dawn / dusk (one angler) Walleye + smallmouth bass Fenwick + 8 lb fluoro leader Light-rod stretch goal Fall trip Walleye is improving as water cools Same Fenwick + 8 lb fluoro Fall is the walleye window

Don't waste midday for walleye — they go deep and inactive in bright sun.

docs.title: Bluegill / Panfish at Potholes (verified specifics)
docs.text: Based on Omnia Fishing patterns + MarDon-area reports. Not generic guesses.

docs.title: WHERE to fish from shore (the actual hotspots)
docs.text:
• "Face of the sand dunes" and "humps in front of the dunes" — verbatim from current Potholes reports for bluegill, crappie, and big perch
  • Channel edges and ledges, 7–14 ft, near the state park — summer pattern
  • Weed edges, 5–10 ft — post-spawn (mid June onward)
  • 2–6 ft over beds, near vegetation — peak spawn (65–75°F water; June typical)

docs.title: BAITS that actually work at Potholes (verified)
docs.text:
• Trout Magnet (Leland's small soft-plastic body on tiny jighead) — specifically named as a Potholes panfish slip-bobber bait by MarDon Resort
  • Strike King Lil Suck'r — specifically named as a Potholes panfish bait
  • Live worms, nightcrawlers — universal but verified as most effective
  • Wax worms — soft body, scent in water, "entices bluegills, crappies, and perch"
  • Crickets, grasshoppers, mealworms — natural alternatives
  • Small leeches — "killer panfish bait" per the sources
  • Color preferences for jigs/plastics: natural baitfish, purple, light neutrals (matches the local forage of small invertebrates, insects, zooplankton, tiny minnows)

docs.title: RIGS that work (verified)
docs.text:
• Slip-bobber rig tipped with Trout Magnet or Lil Suck'r — the MarDon-specific recommendation for Potholes panfish
  • Standard starter bobber rig (specific build):
    • Light rod, 4–6 lb test line (your Fenwick 6.5' Light w/ 4 lb fluoro leader fits; wife's Shakespeare 5.5' combo w/ 6 lb mono also fits)
    • Small Aberdeen hook, size #6 to #8
    • Small bobber 2–3 feet above the hook (snap-on or slip)
    • Bait the hook with worm, wax worm, or Trout Magnet body
    • One small split shot 6" above the hook for sink rate
  • Drop shot + micro jig — summer pattern around dock posts (state park area)
  • Bobber + micro jig over visible beds — spawn

docs.title: What to add to your kit (specifically)
docs.text:
• Leland's Trout Magnet starter kit (jigheads + bodies) — the named Potholes panfish lure
  • Strike King Lil Suck'r (small pack) — second-named panfish bait
  • Small slip bobbers (you already have snap-ons; slip is the verified Potholes rig)
  • Live worms — buy at MarDon Resort, Suncrest, or any bait shop on the drive in. Don't haul from home.
  • Wax worms — for variety; also available locally
  • Colors: lean purple and natural-baitfish for jigs/plastics

You already have or will buy: BB tin split shot ✓ (owned), 6 lb mono / 4 lb fluoro ✓ (owned), snap-on bobbers ✓ (owned). Aberdeen hooks #6 and #8 must be purchased — they're explicitly on the Shopping List under bluegill. The trout-section #10–14 hooks you already own are too small for bluegill rigs.

docs.title: June timing
docs.text: Spawn is in progress when water hits 65°F (typical for June at Potholes). Fish are in 2–6 ft on beds near vegetation, transitioning to weed edges by mid-June. The sand dunes face is the verified hotspot for this window.

docs.title: Walleye Primer (zero-to-functional, for a beginner)
docs.text: Walleye are the marquee fall species at Potholes and worth learning — flaky white meat, mild flavor, one of the best eating freshwater fish. They are NOT like trout. Different habits, different gear, different presentation.

docs.title: What they are
docs.text:
• Cool-water predator (active 45–60°F water — exactly fall conditions at Potholes)
  • Light-sensitive eyes ("walleye" = wall-eye, reflective layer). They hate bright sun.
  • Best at dawn, dusk, after dark, and on cloudy/windy days
  • Structure-oriented: hold near weed edges, rocky points, drop-offs, submerged wood
  • School up — find one, often find more
  • Typical: 14–20"; trophies 24–30"+

docs.title: Daily limits (statewide WA)
docs.text: 8 walleye/day, no minimum size. Verify Potholes-specific rules in current WDFW pamphlet.

docs.title: Gear (works alongside your trout kit)
docs.text:
• Rod: medium-power spinning, 6'6"–7' is ideal. Your Fenwick 6.5' Light will land them but you'll feel under-rodded on a big one.
  • Reel: your Okuma 2500 works
  • Line: 10–15 lb braid mainline → 6–10 lb fluoro leader (clearer water = lighter leader)

docs.title: Your existing rig adaptation (Fenwick + Okuma)
docs.text:
• Swap to 8 lb fluoro leader for walleye trips. Same braid mainline, same rod/reel — just a heavier leader to handle walleye near structure (rocks, weeds, timber). 4 lb fluoro will break off on a hot fish in cover; 8 lb gives you a real shot.
  • Match jig weight to rod: stick with 1/16–1/8 oz jigheads (your rod's sweet spot). Standard walleye sizing is 1/4 oz — castable on the Light rod but suboptimal.
  • Accept the trade-off: you'll land smaller walleye (14–20") just fine and feel every head shake. Big trophies (24"+) will be tense and you'll lose some.
  • Don't force it: if you fall for walleye fishing, upgrade later to a 7' medium-power dedicated walleye rod (~$80–120). Keep the Fenwick Light for trout.

The 8 lb fluoro is on the shopping list anyway (originally for Wallace mackinaw / lowland triploids) — same spool covers walleye trips.

docs.title: Three shore-fishing techniques
docs.text:
1. Jig + soft plastic minnow (the simplest reliable rig)

    • 1/4 oz jighead (round head, ball jig)
    • Soft plastic 3" curl-tail or paddle-tail (white, chartreuse, smoke — Berkley Powerbait Minnow style)
    • Cast out near structure, let it sink to bottom, slow lift-and-drop retrieve back. Pause every 5 seconds — most strikes happen on the fall.
    • This is the most productive shore-fishing walleye rig in WA.

  2. Crankbait cast-and-retrieve

    • Rapala Husky Jerk, Salmo Hornet, or Berkley Flicker Shad — perch and shad color patterns
    • Cast parallel to structure (jetties, drop-offs) and retrieve at medium-slow pace
    • Good for covering water if you don't know where fish are holding

  3. Slip-bobber + jig + minnow (set-and-wait)

    • Slip bobber adjusted to suspend a jig 1–3 ft off bottom
    • Tip jig with a real minnow (allowed in WA — verify Potholes specifics) OR a Berkley Gulp! minnow if you want artificial
    • Cast into productive water and watch the bobber
    • Less active fishing; good while drinking a beer at dusk

docs.title: Shore-fishing locations (the real challenge — most walleye fishing is from boats)
docs.text:
• Jetties and rock structures at boat launches (Potholes SP, Mar Don Resort)
  • Dam area (O'Sullivan Dam) — drop-offs and current
  • Points with structure visible on satellite imagery
  • Weed edges in shallower bays
  • Lights-on docks at night — walleye come in to feed on baitfish attracted by lights

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
• Dawn and dusk are best — the eye thing is real
  • Cloudy or windy days extend the productive window into midday
  • After dark is the secret window — bring a headlamp (red light to preserve night vision)

docs.title: Honest expectation-setting
docs.text:
• Boat anglers consistently outfish shore anglers on walleye
  • Shore-from-Potholes-SP walleye is doable but requires patience, presence at the right times, and casting at structure
  • Plan on a few hours of shore fishing producing maybe 0–3 walleye for a beginner
  • If you want to actually fill a stringer, rent a boat at Mar Don Resort

docs.title: Cleaning + eating
docs.text:
• Skin the fillets (don't scale — too much hassle for thin-skinned walleye)
  • Trim the rib cage out — bony
  • Trim the lateral line if you want to remove the dark "mud line" meat (mild flavor improvement)
  • Pan-fry in butter with light flour/breadcrumb dredge. That's it. Don't overthink it.
  • Walleye is on every "best-tasting freshwater fish" list for a reason.

docs.title: Seep Lakes within Desert WA (short drive from camp)
docs.text:
Created by irrigation seepage after the Columbia Basin Irrigation Project and Potholes Reservoir. Mix of stocked trout, warmwater species, and quality fly-only options.

  • Desert Lake Chain — Harris, Sedge, Tern, Dune lakes; rehabilitated 2010 specifically for rainbow trout
  • Hampton, Soda, Teal, Hutchison, Coyote — varied species; some stocked trout, some bass/panfish
  • Quail Lake — fly fishing only (rule, not just preference)
  • Bobcat and Coyote Creek lakes — largemouth bass, bluegill, crappie

docs.text:

docs.title: Quincy Lakes Wildlife Area Unit
docs.text:
The Quincy Lakes Unit is a piece of the larger Columbia Basin Wildlife Area (160,100 acres total across the Big Bend of the Columbia) — sage, basalt mesas, scattered seep lakes, and irrigation-edge habitat in classic shrub-steppe country west of George in Grant County. ⚠ Critical access caveat for a trailer trip: The main access road through Quincy Lakes Wildlife Area is closed to vehicles October 1 – March 1. Foot traffic is allowed year-round.
