docs.title: Salt Creek Recreation Area
docs.text:
Salt Creek Recreation Area is a Clallam County park on the Strait of Juan de Fuca, about 16 miles west of Port Angeles near Joyce. The campground sits on a grassy bluff with big-water views north to Vancouver Island, and the fishing is genuinely two-in-one: saltwater shore casting on the Strait (Marine Area 6) plus a small coastal stream — Salt Creek itself — running through the park to the beach at Crescent Bay. No boat required; everything here is worked from the beach and rocks.

The catch: the entire park shoreline is a protected tidepool sanctuary. That does not shut down rod-and-reel fishing (see the regulations note below), but it does mean do not remove any tidepool life, shells, rocks, or driftwood — and clams/mussels/oysters are closed year-round.

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
Open in Google Maps →

Tide chart: Salt Creek / Crescent Bay tides →

WDFW Marine Area 6 page: MA 6 – East Juan de Fuca Strait →

docs.title: The Tidepool Sanctuary — What It Does and Doesn't Ban
docs.text:
The whole Salt Creek shoreline (and especially Tongue Point, some of the best tidepool habitat in the state) is a no-take marine protected area under Clallam County Code 23.03.140(6). The ordinance reads:

"It is unlawful for any person or persons to remove driftwood, shells, rocks, or any form of marine life... Marine life is designated as sea stars, anemones, etc. This chapter does not apply to fish caught by sport fishing during season with legal limits."

So, in plain terms:

  • ✅ Rod-and-reel fishing is allowed, and you may keep legal fish (salmon, surfperch, flounder, etc.) taken in season within legal limits and with a license.
  • ❌ Do not remove sea stars, anemones, other tidepool invertebrates, shells, rocks, or driftwood — look, photograph, touch, but leave it.
  • ❌ Shellfish (clams, mussels, oysters) are CLOSED year-round here.
  • ⚠️ Crab is not clearly carved out by the ordinance the way finfish is, and Salt Creek has no pier/dock — treat Dungeness as a boat fishery elsewhere in MA 6, not a shore option here.

docs.title: Prime Shore Spots
docs.text:
• Crescent Bay beach (west of Tongue Point) — the main shore-casting beach, and it's the private half-mile beach fronting Crescent Beach & RV Park — i.e. right out the door of our campsite (see Camping/Logistics). This is the salmon and surfperch water, and it sits west of the Freshwater Bay closure (see salmon note). Best on tide changes.
  • Tongue Point rocks — dramatic structure and tidepools. Fishy-looking, but rockfish are closed and lingcod is out of season in summer; mind the tide and slick rock. Primarily a look-don't-take tidepool spot.
  • Beach gravel along the bluff — surfperch and flounder/sole on a falling tide.
  • Salt Creek mouth / lagoon — sea-run cutthroat stage near the estuary; the creek itself is freshwater (see below). Respect the freshwater salmon closure.

docs.title: Saltwater — Species & Regulations (2026–27, Marine Area 6)
docs.text: Salt Creek is well west of Ediz Hook, in the open portion of MA 6. Always confirm each species at the WDFW MA 6 page or the current pamphlet before fishing — marine seasons are re-set every year.

docs.title: Salmon — the headline shore fishery
docs.text:
• Jul 1 – Aug 15: Open. Hatchery Chinook selective (Chinook min. size 22", adipose-clipped only); other salmon no min. size. Daily limit 2.
  • Aug 16 – Sept 24 and Sept 25 – Oct 15: Open, daily limit 2, release Chinook — this is the coho window.
  • Coho is the realistic shore target from the beach, peaking late August into September.
  • ⚠️ Freshwater Bay closure: the water south of a line from Angeles Point west to Observatory Point (Bachelor Rock) — i.e. the bay east of Tongue Point — is closed to all species July 1 – Oct 31. Fish the Crescent Bay side, west of Tongue Point, which is outside this closure. Confirm the line before casting.
  • Tactics: Buzz Bombs, Pt. Wilson Darts, casting spoons (1/2–3/4 oz Kastmaster/Krocodile) on the incoming tide; first and last hour of light are best.
  • Requires: WA saltwater license plus a salmon Catch Record Card.

docs.title: Surfperch — the reliable summer keeper
docs.text:
• Open year-round. No min. size. Daily limit 10 (shiner perch 15).
  • Tactics: Sand shrimp, mussel, or bloodworm on a high-low rig off the beach gravel; best on a falling tide.

docs.title: Flounder / Sole (flatfish)
docs.text: • "Other Food Fish" — daily limit 2 of each species. Open. Taken on shrimp/worm rigs off the sandy stretches.

docs.title: Sea-run Cutthroat (saltwater)
docs.text: • Present along the beaches and near the creek mouth; light tackle, small spoons/streamers or sand shrimp. Game-fish rules apply — verify current saltwater cutthroat rules (typically release-oriented near stream mouths).

docs.title: Lingcod — CLOSED this weekend
docs.text: • Season: May 1 – June 15 only (min. 26", max. 36", 1/day). Not available in summer.

docs.title: Rockfish — CLOSED
docs.text: • Closed to fishing and retention throughout MA 6. If one comes up incidentally, release it with a descending device.

docs.title: Freshwater — Salt Creek (the stream)
docs.text:
Salt Creek is a small coastal stream, not a destination trout fishery, but it runs through the park and holds coastal (resident) cutthroat, with sea-run cutthroat staging near the mouth in season.

  • Season: WA statewide stream season — open the Saturday before Memorial Day through Oct. 31 (so open this weekend).
  • Salmon & steelhead: freshwater is closed to salmon by default; bull trout/Dolly Varden closed. No special rule was found opening Salt Creek to salmon — treat it as trout only.
  • Trout: No Salt Creek–specific special rule was located. Coastal cutthroat streams commonly require selective gear (single barbless, no bait) and release of wild trout. Safest assumption: catch-and-release, selective gear. ⚠️ Verify the special-rules listing for "Salt Creek (Clallam)" in the current pamphlet before keeping anything.
  • License: WA freshwater (or combo) license.

docs.title: Camping — Crescent Beach & RV Park (our basecamp)
docs.text:
We're staying at the private Crescent Beach & RV Park on Crescent Bay — not the county park next door. It fronts its own half-mile private sandy beach, which is the prime shore-casting/salmon/surfperch water (west of Tongue Point, outside the Freshwater Bay closure), so the good beach is right at the campsite.

  • Sites: tent, partial & full-hookup RV, plus 2 cabins; front-row full-hookup sites have the clearest water/Strait views (Vancouver Island on clear days).
  • Amenities: picnic table + firepit per site, Wi-Fi, laundry, restrooms, hot showers, small store.
  • Reserve: private business, book direct — crescentbeachrv.com. Summer weekends fill; reserve ahead.
  • Location: ~0.5 mi west of Salt Creek Recreation Area — easy walk east to the county park's tidepools (Tongue Point), day-use, and WWII gun-battery ruins.

docs.title: Alpine Trout Loadout (Hike-In, Shore Fishing)
docs.text: Compact kit for Cascade alpine cutthroat / brook / rainbow. Target box: KastKing HyperSeal 3500 (waterproof, double-sided, EVA foam side, includes desiccant — well-suited to backcountry condensation). Plano EDGE 3500 is the smaller minimalist alternative.

docs.title: Current Inventory (owned)
docs.text:
Primary rig (jdosher): * Rod: Fenwick 6.5' Light * Reel: Okuma 2500, spooled with 6 lb hi-vis braid (loaded as mainline) over 6 lb mono backing * Leader: 4 lb fluorocarbon

Second rig (wife's): * Cheap Shakespeare 5.5' combo (rod + reel as a unit, handed down) * Line: 6 lb mono (currently loaded) * Use case: partner trips, casual lake fishing alongside the primary rig * Where it shines: PowerBait + sliding sinker rig for stocked lakes (Patterson, Pearrygin, Cooper, Big Twin); bluegill / sunfish in summer at Potholes; kids' first-fish setup. Short rod = good for tight-bank casting near docks and brush. * Where it doesn't: distance casting (no leverage), big-fish fights (under-powered for walleye / mackinaw / lowland triploids), nymph-style drift work. Don't push it past its lane.

Shared: * Lures: Rooster Tails (assorted) * Bait: PowerBait, rainbow * Scent: Pro-Cure Super Gel — Trophy Trout * Floats: small red/white snap-on bobbers (the spring style)

docs.title: Shopping List (gaps)
docs.text:
• Mepps Aglia #1 — gold (different flash profile from Rooster Tails)
  • Kastmaster spoon — 1/8 oz silver (casts farther in wind, fishes deeper)
  • 8 lb fluorocarbon leader — small spool. Required for walleye trips (Potholes) and useful for Wallace mackinaw / lowland triploids. Swap to this leader, leave the 6 lb braid mainline as-is.
  • Optional second priority: Panther Martin 1/16 oz (yellow/red), casting bubble + a few small flies (Parachute Adams #14–16, olive woolly bugger).

docs.text: A walk-into-Cabelas-and-walk-out list. Sizes/colors tuned for Cascade alpine cutthroat / brook / rainbow.

  • Wets / streamers: olive woolly bugger #10–12, black woolly bugger #10–12

docs.title: Line & terminal
docs.text:
• Mainline: 6 lb hi-vis braid (yellow or chartreuse), 150 yd
  • Backing: existing 6 lb mono fills the bottom of the 2500 spool
  • Leader (alpine default): 4 lb fluorocarbon (owned)
  • Leader (heavier days — Wallace mackinaw, lowland triploids): 8 lb fluorocarbon
  • Small barrel swivels (size 12) — handy for bubble rigs and quick leader swaps
  • Snap swivels: skip — direct knots cast better on light gear

docs.title: Tackle
docs.text:
• Inline spinners (workhorse): 1/16–1/8 oz. Carry variety in flash profile — fish refuse one style, hit another:
    • Rooster Tails (have)
    • Mepps Aglia #0–#2 (gold, silver)
    • Panther Martin (yellow/red, black/yellow)
  • Small spoons: 1/12–1/8 oz Kastmasters or Little Cleos. 2–3 total. Heavier per size — punch through wind and reach deeper holding fish that spinners can't.
  • Bait rigging (set-and-wait while you eat lunch):
    • Aberdeen / octopus hooks #10–14
    • Split shot assortment (BB through #4)
    • Small red/white snap-on bobbers (have) — fine for shallow PowerBait rigs. Slip bobbers are nicer if fishing deeper than ~4 ft.
    • PowerBait rainbow (have) — works on stocked rainbows and cutthroat. Chartreuse is a useful second color.
  • Bubble float + fly: clear casting bubble (half-filled with water = ~1/2 oz) lets you throw a fly on a spinning rod. Solves both the light-lure casting problem and gives you fly presentation on cruising alpine fish.
    • Dries: Parachute Adams #14–16, Elk Hair Caddis
    • Wets / streamers: small woolly buggers (olive / black)
  • Leader: small spool of 4 lb fluorocarbon (have) for tippet/rebuilds. Carry 8 lb fluoro too if heading to Wallace (mackinaw) or lowland triploid lakes.
  • Scent gel (Pro-Cure Super Gel Trophy Trout, owned): pea-sized dab on spinners, spoons, or soft plastics. Reapply every 15–20 min. Skip on PowerBait (already scented).

docs.title: Paper (the stuff that gets you cited)
docs.text:
• WA fishing license — phone screenshot is fine but carry printed copy in a zip-top; cell service vanishes
  • Catch record card if targeting anything that requires one (usually not alpine trout — verify)
  • Trailhead pass (NWFP or Discover Pass) — easy to forget at the door

docs.title: Rigs (the productive setups)
docs.text:
• Sliding-sinker dough rig (PowerBait / Power Eggs): mainline → small sliding egg sinker (¼–½ oz) → small barrel swivel → ~18" of 4 lb fluoro leader → #14–16 small treble hook molded with a marble of PowerBait. The dough floats off the bottom; the sinker pins to bottom; cruising trout find it. The "soak while you eat lunch" rig.
  • Trout worm / Mice Tail rig: #8–10 baitholder hook with the soft bait threaded on → one small split shot 18" up the line → optional small slip bobber 3–5 ft up if fishing deeper than the lure can suspend itself. Cast and let it drift, or work it slowly back.
  • Curl-tail grub / soft plastic rig: 1/32–1/16 oz jighead → 1.5–2" curl-tail grub → cast and slow-roll back. Active presentation; works trout AND yellow perch off the same rod.
  • Bubble + fly rig: clear casting bubble half-filled with water → 3–6 ft of 4 lb fluoro leader → small fly (dry, wet, or streamer). Solves both the light-lure casting problem and gives you fly presentation on a spinning rod.

docs.title: Line & Casting Light Lures
docs.text:
For 1/16 oz lures specifically (Rooster Tails, small spinners), the line is what limits you more than rod/reel:

  • Mainline: 6 lb hi-vis braid (yellow or green). Thin as 1–2 lb mono = casts ultralight lures dramatically better. Hi-vis is fine because the fluoro leader handles fish-side stealth.
  • Leader: 3–4 ft of 4 lb fluoro. (8 lb for bigger-fish days.)
  • Knot — braid to fluoro: Double Uni (easy, reliable). FG knot is technically better but overkill here.
  • Knot — fluoro to lure: Improved Clinch or Palomar.
  • Spool loading: put existing 6 lb mono as backing first to fill ~half the deep 2500 spool, top with braid to within 1/8" of the spool lip.

Casting technique for 1/16 oz: * Pendulum / lob cast, not a snap — let the rod tip load on the back swing. * Open the bail before the lure stalls at the apex. * Sidearm sweep for accuracy under trees. * Cast with the wind — even 5 mph headwind kills light lures. * When wind or distance is the problem: rig the casting bubble + small spinner or fly (above).

docs.text:

  • Big crankbaits, jigs heavier than 1/16 oz, bass-sized terminal tackle

docs.title: Non-Toxic Shotgun Ammo
docs.text: Personal default: use non-toxic everywhere, even where lead is still legal. Simpler kit, no rule-checking at the trailhead, no lead in the field.

docs.title: Steel vs Bismuth — Field Reality
docs.text:
Steel is what most Columbia Basin hunters actually use (~70%+ of vests in the parking lot). Bismuth is the premium minority pick.

Steel (the field default) Bismuth (the premium pick) Cost / box of 25 $20–25 $40–75 (2–3× steel) Density 7.8 g/cc 9.6 g/cc (close to lead) Pattern behavior Tighter than lead — go larger shot Lead-like Choke compatibility OK on modern guns (IC, Modified); avoid tight chokes on older barrels Safe through any choke Best for Modern guns, cost-conscious hunters, high-volume shooters Old fixed-choke guns, classic SxS, low-volume hunters who want lead-like behavior Field share ~70%+ of Columbia Basin upland hunters Minority premium pick

For a modern Bobwhite G2 or Setter LT (steel-rated through Modified): steel is the smart-money default. Bismuth is a "fancy day" option.

docs.title: My Default Load for Desert WA Quail
docs.text:
Steel #6, 20g, 2 3/4" shell, 3/4 oz OR 7/8 oz payload — whichever is on the shelf. Both work for quail.

  • Why steel #6: the field-standard size for Columbia Basin quail; widely stocked
  • Why 2 3/4" NOT 3": 3" shells are 1+ oz payloads — heavier recoil, overkill for quail ranges. The Bobwhite at 6 lbs will let you feel 3" loads. 2 3/4" is the upland standard.
  • Payload choice — 3/4 oz vs 7/8 oz:
    • 3/4 oz = ~137 pellets of #6 steel. Lighter recoil. Less meat damage. Commonly labeled "Target" but functionally fine for quail.
    • 7/8 oz = ~160 pellets. Standard hunting spec; more margin if your gun is patterning loose.
    • For quail at 15–25 yards, both work. Many quail-specific hunters prefer the 3/4 oz for the lighter recoil.

Picked load: Winchester Xpert Upland Steel 20g 2 3/4" 3/4 oz #6.

  • Lower velocity (~1300–1350 fps) than Federal Upland (~1500+ fps) → less recoil through the 6 lb Bobwhite SxS — pleasant across a full hunt's worth of shots
  • ~$3/box cheaper than Federal Upland
  • Plenty of energy at 15–25 yard quail range
  • Skip Federal Speed-Shok (labeled "waterfowl," not upland-tuned)

Other acceptable in-stock alternatives: * Federal Upland Steel 20g 2 3/4" 3/4 oz #6 — if Xpert is out; hotter load = more recoil * Kent Fasteel 20g 2 3/4" #6 * Remington Sport Loads 20g 2 3/4" 3/4 oz #6

Cost: $20–25/box of 25 at any Cabela's / Sportsman's / Bi-Mart.

Premium upgrade option: Boss Bismuth 20g 2 3/4" 7/8 oz #7.5 if you want lead-like pattern density on a "special day" hunt. ~$40/box.

docs.title: Where Non-Toxic Is REQUIRED in WA
docs.text:
• Columbia Basin Wildlife Area Complex (Banks Lake, Gloyd Seeps, Lower Crab Creek, Quincy Lakes, Warden, Desert units) — all game birds and game animals
  • Any pheasant release site — statewide
  • All waterfowl hunting — federal rule

Penalty for lead in required areas: $1,000 mandatory fine + 2-year loss of small game privileges.

docs.text: Material Cost / box of 25 Pattern behavior Choke compatibility Notes Steel $20–30 Patterns tighter than lead — go 1 shot size larger Modified or more open on older barrels; verify steel rating Cheapest; what most hunters use for waterfowl Bismuth $35–45 Lead-like — soft, dense, behaves naturally Safe through any choke Premium pick for upland; lead-like performance without the $$$ of TSS Hevi-Metal / Hevi-Bismuth blends $30–35 Middle ground Mostly choke-safe; verify Mid-budget, decent performance Tungsten Super Shot (TSS) $50+ Densest available, smallest shot can punch Safe through any choke Overkill for upland; turkey/waterfowl specialist

docs.title: California / Valley Quail
docs.text:
• Range: 15–25 yard flushes typical
  • What to look for: pattern density at close range beats raw energy
  • Shot size: #7.5 or #8 (the common-shelf sizes) for either steel or bismuth
  • Payload: 7/8 oz to 1 oz
  • Specific picks:
    • Boss Bismuth 20g 7/8 oz #7.5 ($35–45) — the classic quail size, lead-like behavior, premium pick
    • Federal Speed-Shok Steel 20g 7/8 oz #7 or smaller ($20–25) — workhorse but check stock; non-toxic #7 is genuinely scarce on shelves
    • Federal Bismuth 20g 7/8 oz #7.5 — alternative bismuth source
    • Hevi-Metal Pheasant 20g 7/8 oz ($30–35) — multi-species option

Availability note: non-toxic shells commonly stock #4, #5, #6, #7.5, #8 — #7 is uncommon in the non-toxic world (it's a lead-load convention that didn't carry over). Plan around #7.5 and #8 for the small-shot end.

Why #7.5 specifically for quail: more energy per pellet than #8, more pellets per ounce than #6 — it's the classic quail balance many upland hunters use.

docs.title: Chukar
docs.text:
• Range: 25–40 yards typical (open canyon country)
  • What to look for: more energy than quail loads; tougher bird
  • Shot size: #5 or #6 steel, OR #5 or #6 bismuth
  • Payload: 1 oz
  • Specific picks:
    • Federal Speed-Shok Steel 20g 1 oz #5 — energy at range
    • Boss Bismuth 20g 1 oz #6 ($40+) — premium, won't fail on a tough crossing chukar
    • Hevi-Metal 20g 1 oz #6 ($30–35) — solid all-around

docs.title: Hungarian (Gray) Partridge
docs.text:
• Range: 25–40 yards (similar to chukar)
  • Same loads as chukar work — #5 or #6 steel/bismuth, 1 oz payload

docs.title: Pheasant (if you hunt mixed bag at Desert WA / Methow)
docs.text:
• Range: 30–45 yards typical
  • Shot size: #4 or #5 steel, OR #5 bismuth
  • Payload: 1 oz minimum; 1 1/8 oz preferred if your gun handles it (most 20g O/Us do not)
  • Honest 20g limitation: pheasant are at the edge of 20g territory. For a pheasant-focused day, the 12g pump is the better tool.

docs.title: Forest Grouse (Ruffed, Dusky/Blue, Spruce)
docs.text:
• Range: 15–25 yards in timber; close flushes
  • What to look for: dense pattern at close range; small shot doesn't damage the meat as much
  • Shot size: #6, #7.5, or #8 (skip #7 — uncommon in non-toxic)
    • Ruffed grouse in tight cover: #7.5 or #8
    • Blue/dusky in more open subalpine: #6 or #7.5
  • Material: Bismuth is the smart pick — open chokes are common in grouse cover, and bismuth doesn't damage meat at close range
  • Specific picks:
    • Boss Bismuth 20g 7/8 oz #7.5 — close-cover ruffed; the classic grouse size
    • Federal Speed-Shok Steel 20g 7/8 oz #6 — workable cheap option
    • Hevi-Metal 20g 7/8 oz — middle-ground
  • Non-toxic not required in most forest grouse habitat (USFS / DNR land), but using bismuth here standardizes your kit

docs.title: By Species — 12 Gauge Loads (recoil-equivalent to 20g, for the converted 870)
docs.text:
Same species, but drop payload to 1 oz (not the standard 1 1/8 oz) to keep recoil closer to 20g.

Species 12g shot size 12g payload Notes Quail Steel #6 or #7, bismuth #7 1 oz Pattern density Chukar Steel #5, bismuth #6 1 oz More energy than quail Hun partridge Steel #5, bismuth #6 1 oz Same as chukar Pheasant Steel #4, bismuth #5 1 oz or 1 1/8 oz 12g advantage shows here Forest grouse Bismuth #7 or #8 1 oz Bismuth preferred

docs.title: Choke + Non-Toxic Notes
docs.text:
• Steel patterns 1 constriction tighter than lead. Lead Modified ≈ steel Improved Cylinder.
  • Bismuth patterns like lead — use your lead-era choke choices.
  • Never run steel through fixed full choke on older barrels — risk of damage. Use IC or skeet with steel.

docs.title: Pre-Trip Checklist
docs.text:
• Buy non-toxic at least a week before the trip — local sporting goods can be picked over in fall
  • Pattern-test at 20 and 30 yards on butcher-paper before trusting the load on birds
  • Keep receipt/box label photo in your hunting kit — proof you bought non-toxic if asked
  • Standardize loads across the kit if using non-toxic everywhere — easier to grab, easier to predict

docs.title: Dark Sky Sites for Combo Trips
docs.text: Camping + fishing + stargazing locations, filtered by travel time from Shoreline. Bortle scale: 1 = darkest, 9 = brightest urban; useful naked-eye Milky Way starts ~3, deep-sky scope work really opens up at 2.

docs.title: Methow Valley (WA) — Bortle 2–3 — the primary local target
docs.text: Closest serious combo destination from Shoreline (~4–5 hrs via Hwy 20 when open; ~5 hrs via Hwy 2 + Blewett year-round). Eastside rain shadow → far more clear nights than the westside. The trifecta in one valley: - Astronomy: Mazama / Winthrop area is genuinely dark; widefield Milky Way unobscured; Andromeda visible naked-eye. - Fishing: Patterson Lake (trout, shore-fishable), Pearrygin Lake State Park (trout, camping on site), Methow River (resident cutthroat). - Hunting (fall): Methow Wildlife Area — California quail, chukar partridge, ruffed and blue grouse. One of the best upland bird destinations in WA. - Camping: Pearrygin Lake SP (developed, lake access), Methow Valley dispersed sites along Twisp and Chewuch river roads.

docs.title: Goldendale Observatory area (WA) — Bortle 2
docs.text: South-central WA, Klickitat County. IDA-designated International Dark Sky Park. Camping at Brooks Memorial State Park nearby. Limited fishing emphasis vs Methow, but the observatory itself is worth a visit on its own.

docs.title: Sun Lakes / Steamboat Rock (Eastern WA) — Bortle 3
docs.text: Channeled Scablands south of Coulee Dam. ~4 hrs. Sun Lakes-Dry Falls SP has trout/bass and developed camping. Not the darkest skies on this list but a balanced midpoint.

docs.title: Sullivan Lake / Salmo-Priest (NE WA Selkirks) — Bortle 1–2
docs.text: ~6–7 hrs. Closest genuine Bortle-1 site reachable from Seattle. Sullivan Lake holds trout and kokanee; developed lakeside camping. The darkness pays off for galaxy / faint-nebula work — M51 spiral arms, the Veil with an OIII filter, etc.

docs.title: Central Idaho Dark Sky Reserve — Stanley / Sawtooth (ID) — Bortle 1
docs.text: ~8–10 hrs. One of the largest dark sky reserves in the world. Sawtooth alpine lakes for cutthroat; Stanley Lake and Redfish Lake camping. Pilgrimage destination — plan around new moon and make it a week.

docs.title: Steens Mountain (SE Oregon) — Bortle 1
docs.text: ~10+ hrs. True wilderness sky. Donner und Blitzen River native redband trout. BLM camping at Frenchglen. Long haul, but the kind of darkness most people never see.

docs.title: Sites to Skip (Astronomically) Despite Being Close
docs.text:
• Mountain Loop Hwy — Everett light dome, Bortle 4–5
  • Hwy 2 corridor (Stevens Pass and lakes) — same problem
  • Olympic Peninsula west side — dark on paper, but coastal humidity/fog kills many nights
  • Edmonds Pier / Puget Sound urban shoreline — Bortle 6–7

docs.title: Planning Tools
docs.text:
• lightpollutionmap.info — Bortle overlay on any map
  • darksitefinder.com — community-curated dark site database
  • Clear Outside (app) — cloud cover, transparency, seeing forecast tuned for astronomers
  • Astrospheric (app) — alternative weather forecasting; some PNW astronomers prefer it
  • Stellarium (free planetarium) — plan targets the night before

docs.title: Gear Notes — 150mm Dobsonian
docs.text:
• Well-matched to car-camping astronomy: no power, minimal setup, packs compactly.
  • Optimal observing window: new moon ± 3 nights. Plan camping trips around the new-moon calendar — full-moon stargazing is wasted travel.
  • Pack: red headlamp, eyepiece case (don't leave eyepieces loose in a car!), observing chair, eyepiece dew shield, planisphere or planetarium app, warm layers (alpine summer nights drop below freezing).
  • A simple Telrad finder + a 25mm and 10mm eyepiece is enough for one trip; resist over-packing accessories.

docs.title: Field Notes
docs.text: • Track Bortle estimate (your eyes vs the maps), seeing, transparency, and what was visible. Use this to calibrate which sites are worth which drive times.

docs.title: Fishing Knots (Field Card)
docs.text:
Uni — line to terminal tackle · Uni Snell — line to bait hook · Alberto — braid to leader · Double Palomar — braid to swivel. Wet every knot before cinching. Diagrams: John E. Sherry / netknots.com.

Printable 1-page card (PDF) — all four knots, letter size.

docs.title: Double Palomar Knot
docs.text: Braid to snap swivel. Tie the Palomar below, but repeat steps 3–4 — a second overhand wrap through the same loop — before passing the loop over the swivel. That second wrap is the only difference, and it's what keeps slick braid from slipping.

docs.title: Shopping List
docs.text: Compact, printable tackle reference organized by target species. Each line: item — what it's for.

docs.title: TROUT — alpine cutthroat, brook, rainbow
docs.text:
Line - 6 lb hi-vis braid, 150 yd — mainline; thin as 1–2 lb mono, casts ultralight lures - 4 lb fluorocarbon, small spool — primary leader - 8 lb fluorocarbon — heavier leader for Wallace mackinaw, lowland triploids

Spinners (1/16–1/8 oz) - Mepps Aglia #0, #1 (gold, silver) — different flash profile than Rooster Tails - Panther Martin 1/16 oz (yellow/red, black/yellow) — tight vibration alternative - Rooster Tails (yellow coachdog, brown trout) — workhorse, already owned

Spoons - Kastmaster 1/12, 1/8 oz (silver, gold) — punches through wind, fishes deeper - Little Cleo 1/8 oz (frog, nickel) — wider wobble, slow retrieves

Bait rig (PowerBait / worms) - Aberdeen or octopus hooks #10–14 — small-hook rig for soft baits - Small treble hooks #14–16 — for dough on the sliding-sinker rig - Sliding egg sinkers, ¼–½ oz — sliding-sinker dough rig - Small barrel swivels size 12 — stop the sliding sinker - Tin split shot, BB (non-toxic, ~100/pack) — workhorse single size; stack 2–3 for more weight. Treat as single-use (tin fractures when re-opened). - Small slip bobbers — PowerBait deeper than ~4 ft - PowerBait chartreuse — second color beyond rainbow

Imitation baits / soft plastics (active fishing, no live bait required) - PowerBait Trout Worms 3" (pink shad, bubblegum, motor oil) — most versatile add to dough - PowerBait Mice Tails — deadly on stocked rainbows; single-hook rig - Curl-tail grubs 1.5–2" (chartreuse, white, smoke) on 1/32–1/16 oz jigheads — works trout AND yellow perch - Berkley Gulp! Earthworms or Maggots — softer scent alternative to PowerBait - PowerBait Power Eggs — pairs with rainbow dough on egg+dough rig

Bubble + fly (force multiplier on light spinning gear) - Clear casting bubbles — adds ½ oz casting mass, throws flies on spin rod - Parachute Adams #14–16 — primary dry - Elk Hair Caddis #14 — secondary dry - Olive + black woolly buggers #10–12 — wet / streamer

Terminal - Barrel swivels size 12 — bubble rigs, quick leader swaps - Single Siwash hooks (open-eye), sizes #4–#8 — replace trebles on Rooster Tails / Mepps / Kastmasters for selective-gear water (Beckler, SF Sky tribs). Mustad 9510XS or Owner Cutting Point are the standards. - Split-ring pliers (small) — open the split ring on a lure to swap treble → siwash cleanly

Tools - Forceps / hemostats — barbless hook removal - Line snips on a zinger — knots, retying - Stainless steel fishing scissors — cut braid cleanly, trim soft plastics to size, snip bait

Yellow perch crossover — same rod/reel/line works; just add smaller hooks (#6–10) and a slip bobber + jig + worm rig.

Bluegill / panfish crossover (Potholes shore + lowland lakes — verified Potholes-specific) - Aberdeen hooks #6 and #8 — REQUIRED for the standard bluegill bobber rig (your existing #10-14 hooks are too small for the bluegill rig) - Leland's Trout Magnet starter kit (jighead + body) — named-by-MarDon as the Potholes panfish slip-bobber bait - Strike King Lil Suck'r — second named-by-MarDon panfish bait at Potholes - Small slip bobbers — Potholes-verified rig style; complements the snap-on bobbers you already own - Color lean: purple and natural-baitfish (verified Potholes preference) - Live worms / wax worms — buy locally at MarDon Resort or any bait shop on the drive in - Berkley Crappie Nibbles or Gulp! Maggots — long-shelf-life backup if no live bait

docs.title: FLOUNDER / SOLE — Puget Sound piers & beaches
docs.text:
Hooks - Octopus or wide-gap circle hooks #2 to 1/0 — hi/low rig staple (scale to 2/0 for bigger starry flounder) - Long-shank baitholder #2 to 1/0 — easier removal, holds soft bait better

Weights - Pyramid sinkers 2–4 oz — holds in current - Bank sinkers 2–4 oz — mild current or sand bottom

Rig components - Pre-tied dropper-loop hi/low leaders — fastest setup - 3-way swivels size 4 — build your own hi/low - 15–20 lb fluoro leader spool — abrasion resistance against pier structure - Bead-chain swivels — reduce line twist on current-driven rigs

Bait - Sand shrimp (frozen) — premium flatfish bait, soaks well - Squid strips — cheap, durable, all-day soak - Herring strips — small slivers; pair well with shrimp - Bloodworms / sandworms — top-tier bait but pricey

Optional - Sabiki rig (size 8–10) — catch fresh herring on site for cut bait - Bait knife / scissors — strip cutting - Latex / nitrile gloves — slime and bait handling

Future sections to add as we build them out: LINGCOD, SQUID, SALMON (coho/pink), UPLAND BIRD.

docs.title: ⚠ Personal preference: extractors only
docs.text:
Strong preference for extractors over ejectors — no flying cases (quieter, no littering, don't lose shells). This rules out:

  • ❌ CZ Teal — has auto-ejectors despite the great $550 price. Skip.
  • ❌ CZ Redhead Premier (Teal's parent gun) — same reason.

Viable CZ options under this constraint: Bobwhite G2 (SxS), Drake (O/U), Mallard (basic O/U). Verify Upland Ultralight at the counter — newer SKUs may have ejectors.

docs.title: The Teal at $550 — value pick if ejectors are acceptable (they're NOT for jdosher)
docs.text:
The CZ Teal is the Cabela's-exclusive rebadge of the CZ Redhead Premier — a higher-tier gun than the Drake at a discount. Mid-tier internals (mechanical trigger, mid rib + vent rib, better wood, 5 chokes, auto-ejectors) at entry-tier money.

For jdosher: skip the Teal. Auto-ejectors violate the personal preference rule. The $400 discount over the Redhead Premier means nothing when the underlying gun isn't a fit. (Catch is also that at 6.9 lbs in 20g, the Teal is heavier than alternatives — but the ejector issue is the disqualifier.)

docs.title: Standout pick — TriStar Hunter EX LT
docs.text:
On paper, the Hunter EX LT is the best match for jdosher's profile:

  • 5.4 lbs — lighter than CZ Upland Ultralight (6 lbs), CZ Drake (6.5), and the Teal (6.9). For all-day walking in shrub-steppe, this is a real difference.
  • Extractors — matches preference
  • ~$700 MSRP, often $600 street — competitive with Drake
  • Aluminum alloy receiver w/ steel inserts, chrome-lined barrels, fiber optic front sight, sealed action
  • Single selective trigger, 5 Beretta-pattern choke tubes

Honest caveats (real, not marketing):

  • TriStar QC reputation is mixed — Turkish budget gun; some buyers report wood-to-metal fit issues, occasional misfires on early-life rounds. Lifetime warranty handles most issues but expect potential break-in pains.
  • 5.4 lbs comes at a cost — light guns kick more for the same load. Plan on lighter 7/8 oz steel loads for comfortable shooting; 1 oz+ loads will be noticeable.
  • The LT alloy receiver is durable but not "heirloom" feel — this is a working gun, not a generational gun.

If you'd rather have a slightly heavier but more robust gun with similar extractor design: TriStar Hunter EX (standard steel receiver) at 6.3 lbs and ~$550–650. Same ergonomics, more weight to soak recoil, lower price.

docs.title: Current Working Pick
docs.text:
Leaning: CZ Bobwhite G2 SxS, 20 gauge, ~$680 at Sportsman's Warehouse. 6 lbs, extractors, color case-hardened receiver, double-trigger or single-trigger option, English straight stock option, lifetime warranty.

Why this pivoted from the Setter LT: - "Not poor — don't want to go that cheap" — the LT is a working/disposable gun - SxS is arguably the better tool for traditional upland walking (balance, lighter feel, instant choke selection on double trigger, extractors are SxS-native) - CZ QC is more refined than TriStar's Turkish-budget reputation - Bobwhite at $680 is the value sweet spot for new SxS

Fallback options if the Bobwhite doesn't mount well in person: - TriStar Setter LT 20g 28" at $475 — interim O/U - TriStar Setter S/T 26" at $475 — heavier O/U sibling - CZ Drake at $700–800 — extractor O/U

Real upgrade path (if the SxS bug bites): - CZ Sharp-Tail SxS at $1,000–1,500 — refined extractor SxS - Dickinson Plantation Turkish SxS at $1,200–1,800 - Used quality vintage SxS (Browning BSS, SKB, vintage Beretta) at $800–1,500

docs.title: Premium-Tier Reality for Extractor-Only O/Us
docs.text:
The extractor-only constraint largely closes off the standard premium O/U tier. Almost every gun in the $1,000–3,000+ O/U bracket comes with auto-ejectors as standard (Beretta 686 Silver Pigeon, Browning Citori line, Franchi Instinct SL, Caesar Guerini, all the Italian-builds).

Premium extractor-only paths exist mostly on the SxS side:

  • CZ Sharp-Tail (SxS, ~$1,000–1,500) — known extractor-only quantity, upland-classic
  • Dickinson Plantation Turkish SxS (~$1,200–1,800) — mid-tier extractor SxS
  • Connecticut Shotgun Manufacturing RBL (~$5,000+) — high-end American SxS
  • Used quality vintage O/U with original extractors — niche hunt; pre-ejector-era guns

If "spend more for a better gun" is the goal under this constraint, the upgrade path is to SxS, not a fancier O/U.

docs.title: Decision after extractor filter
docs.text:
The viable shortlist (with weight savings vs current 12g pumps):

Gun Weight Savings vs Mossberg 500 (7.15 lbs) Savings vs Remington 870 (7.6 lbs) Price TriStar Hunter EX LT 5.4 lbs −1.75 lbs −2.20 lbs ~$600–700 CZ Bobwhite G2 (SxS) ~6.0 lbs −1.15 lbs −1.60 lbs $700–800 TriStar Hunter EX (standard) 6.3 lbs −0.85 lbs −1.30 lbs $550–650 CZ Drake (O/U) 6.5 lbs −0.65 lbs −1.10 lbs $700–800 Stoeger Condor I 6.9 lbs −0.25 lbs −0.70 lbs $559

Reality of weight savings on the trail: carrying ~2 lbs less for 5–6 hours of walking shrub-steppe is the difference between "tired but fine" and "wanting to shoot a 30-yard pheasant from a sitting position." For dogless walking trips this is the single biggest gear-comfort factor.

Honest decision after weight + extractor filter:

  1. TriStar Hunter EX LT — best on-paper match (lightest + extractors + reasonable price). Accept TriStar QC variability and lighter felt-recoil.
  2. CZ Drake — give up 1.1 lbs vs the LT for better build reputation and refinement.
  3. CZ Bobwhite G2 — SxS option that still saves 1.6 lbs vs the 870.
  4. Stoeger Condor I — $559 budget play but only saves 0.7 lbs vs the 870 — barely worth it for the upland-feel upgrade.

docs.title: Decision Framework (Updated)
docs.text:
CZ Teal @ $550 — the value pick: * You're not weight-obsessed (0.5–1 lb heavier than alternatives) * You want mid-tier internals at entry-tier money — mechanical trigger, better rib setup, refined feel * You like the gloss black look (or don't care that it's different from the standard silver Redhead) * You'd otherwise spend $700 on the Drake — the Teal is objectively a better gun at less money

CZ Drake @ $700–800 — the standard O/U: * You want simpler, more "standard" CZ O/U * You may want easier resale (Drake is a more common known quantity than the Cabela's-exclusive Teal)

CZ Upland Ultralight @ $800–900 — the lightweight pick: * All-day walking matters most — you'll feel the 1 lb difference vs the Teal * Worth the $300+ premium over the Teal for the weight savings

CZ Bobwhite G2 @ $700–800 — the romantic pick: * You specifically want the SxS experience * Aesthetic + tradition matter as much as performance

Stoeger Condor / Yildiz O/U @ $450–550 — the budget alternatives: * If you'd buy the Teal but don't want to commit even $550 to a "trying it out" purchase * Real working guns, just less refined than the Teal

docs.title: Honest Take on the Teal
docs.text:
At $550, the Teal probably wins the price/value question outright among CZ O/Us — you're paying entry-tier money for mid-tier internals. The 6.9 lb weight is the real trade-off; for shrub-steppe walking (Desert WA's mostly flat-to-rolling terrain, not steep chukar canyons), this is tolerable. For Wenas rimrock chukar climbs it would matter more.

Go to Cabela's, mount the Teal, and shoulder/swing it. Spec sheet says it's the value winner; only your face and shoulder can tell you if it fits. If it does, $550 is the buy.

If you find it nose-heavy or the stock doesn't fit, the Upland Ultralight is the obvious upgrade path (lighter + alloy receiver + still easier sight picture than SxS).
